div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.

OBJECT LESSONS. Last week's item headed " Lymm children among the bees" reminded me of a period not very hr back when I had the pleasure of conducting several such parties through the printing works where was pro- duced a newspaper of which I was editor at the time. I had inserted an invitation to elementary school teachers to bring their charges on any day that might be mutually convenient, and, as an afternoon spent in that way counts as ordinary school attendance, many availed themselves of the opportunity. I generally received the visitors on publication day, when I was at liberty to go over the establishment with them and explain the process of newspaper production. The youngsters, who bad been prepared by a special lesson beforehand, were mostly keen and appreciative. They were particularly interested in the Iynot3pe indeed, any adult who has not previously seen one at work invariably is and well may be. MY DOUBLE. That Lymm "horse with a double" brought to my mind certain amusing incidents which occurred in my own experience while residing in a Lancashire town some years ago. I had a double who was local superintendent for the Pludential Assur- ance Society, and as I walla(' along the street strangers would accost me on the supposition that I was the insurance man. "Oh, Mr s 11--," one would say, "I got that postcard of your's," and, as the easiest way out of the difficulty, I would simply say "All right" and pass on. Once, when I happened to have leisure, I yielded to the impulse to carry the joke further. The collector cf income tax for the distict button-holed me with "That return you've just made will never do, you know:' " Indeed," said I, " what's amiss? " " Well," said he "the form is at my place. I could explain better if you would step across with me and look at it." A few " moments later I found myself in the collector's office amid a bewildering maze cf documents and red tape. Taking down a bundle of the papers which even the mcst fortunate among us so much dread, he selected cue of formidable bulk and was about to cross-examine me respecting certain details when I interposed the objection that it. did not bear my name. " But," said the one who had taken me to task on account of alleged errors which were not mine at all, " surely you are Mr. ? " "Oh dear, no," I replied, "My name's 11--" He apologised profusely as he bowed me out; he really was a very polite tax- gatherer indeed. APT QUOTATIONS. Councillor Jenkins' euotation of " Cleanliness is next to godliness " as from "the Old Book " serves at least to remind one that some of the most familiar of the tags in daily use are derived from Ecclesiastes, Jeremiah, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, and other books of the Bible, especially Proverbs. Among well-known ones from the latter are "A soft answer turneth sway , wrath," " Fools hate knowledge," " Go to the ant, ,1 thou sluggard, consider her ways and be wise," "Spare 11 the rod, spoil the child," " Heap coals of fire upon: his head," "Hope deferred makes the heart sick." In the New Testament we find quotations from the Old. St. Paul speaks of " Heaping coals of fire" He is also responsible for " In the twinkling of an eye," " As a man sows, so shall he reap," " To the pure all things are pure." And so one might go on till the column were filled. "CLEANLINESS . • . GODLINESS." The lapse into which the Warrington Councillor was betrayed last week is fairly common, and examples might easily be multiplied. Thus the expression "mess of pottage," supposed to be a quotation from the Bible, never appears in it, or in the Prayer Book, or in any of the formularies of the Church. When, as a youth, I joined a mutual improvement society, I met with this edifying example during a discussion on total abstinence, the speaker being a middle-aged man: "Mr. Chairman, I think that, connected with a Christian Church as we all are, we need not spend any more time debating a point that has been decided for us by an authority that we are bound to admit as supreme and unerring. At all events, it is enough hr me that the Bible distinctly lays it down that " water

Is best." DIFFERENT EXAMPLES. Yes, yes ; Councillor Jenkins sinned in good com- pany. It has been urged with some show of reason, indeed, that certain quotations are authorised by high authorities. Byron wrote : " In pride of place 'here last the eagle flew," adding a footn( te : " In pride of place' is a term of falconry, and means the highest pitch of fight. See 'Macbeth,' etc. : ' An eagle towering in his pride of place.", But never have men gone hawking with eagles. What Shakespeare wrote was : "A falcon, towering in her pride of place." However as someone has observed, Byron was not always as careful as he might have been. Does he not, in his Paddy Blake's echo in The Bride of Abydos," cry : " Bark to the hurried question of Despair : • Where is my child ? ' An echo answers 'Where ?' " whereas the echo would have answered "child." This has led to •a good deal of confusion ; speakers and writers are continually representing echo as returning impossible answers:Now and again,of course,it ispluinly a matter of downright ignorance, as in the experience of a gentleman who was naturally rather startled when an eloquent chairman introduced him as the " putative candidate " for a constituency. Many laughable instances have come under my notice. Not long ago •' Punch " had this : lie : "Very interesting these Morris-dances. Have you seen any before ? " She : No. I don't even know who Morris was." Inside as well as outside Council chambers there are people capable of perpetrating such things as that. A HEALTH POINT.

One of the health points in laat week's" Examiner " bids 1.18 not blame the window lreaking suffragette, inasmuch as "she only wants to make air common property.- I know a son:•ewhat eccentric and happily

div.p: Phone 79

fairly well-to-do parson who, on entering a sick room from which fresh air has been carefully excluded,often contrives to smash a window with his walkingstick accidentally, of course. Then he will say : "Really. how clumsy cf me. Of course, I'll see that it is repaired ; leave it to me." A few days later, he calla to find that the glazier has not yet made good the damage. The work is done ultimately, but by that time the patient, if not well enough to be downstairs, has become so accustomed to fresh air that the window has to be opened. THE BARE IDEA!

In his delightful and ever-welcome Parish Magazine the Rev. A. M. Mitchell writes to the above effect con- cerning the beardless. All the same, the time to advocate the disestablishment of the barber is not yet. So long ago as 1583, Phillip Stubbs ra rote in his " Anatomie of abuses " :—" Barbers are Ter ie necessarie, for otherwise men should grow verie ongglisom and deformed, and their haire would in processe of time overgrowe their faces, rather like monsters than comlie, sober Christians. I cannot but marvell at the beastliness of some ruffians that will have their haire to grow over their faces like monsters and savage people— Lay, rather like mad- men, hanging downs their shoulders like women's haire doth, which is a shams and reproach, as the apostle proveth" I may be told that this refers more to the hair of the head than to the beard. Sooth to say, there are other considerations. I read, for instance, that Elnathan Sherman, a farmer, eighty- two years of age, of Rock, Massachusetts, who has never been shaved, estimates that by allowing his beard to grow he has saved as much money as an ordinary farmer accumulates from all sources in a lifetime. He has missed 22,000 shaves, which, with tips, would have cost him £6OO, snd would have taken in all nine months to perform. THE HEARTLESS GUNNER.

The Frenchman represents the Englishman as Baying "It's a fine day ; let's go out and kill some- thing." Alas, there is truth in the gibe. I can imagine how some even in Warrington longed to have a shot at that eagle, or whatever it was, that paid the town a flying visit last week, and perched for a rest on the Parish Church spire. What a farce the so-called Wild Birds Protection Act is ! I know bipeds who openly boast of shooting king fishers, cuckoos, and many smaller birds ; and I am acquainted with creatures w ho, not content t draw the line at plover's eggs, must neeos have a dish of larks on the menu. Then there are the gamekeepers, the farmers, and the irresponsible small boys, who, from various mistaken motives or for no reason at all, have done their best to deprive the countryside of various species of its feathered inhabitants.

div.head: LATE MR P. T. WINSKILL.
div.p: THE LATE MR P. T. WINSKILL.

The. older generation of Warrington people will doubtless regret to hear of the death of Mr. P. T. Winskill, a former resident and active worker in this town. Mr. Winskill came to Warrington early in 1871 and for some years was a very ardent advocate and agent for the total abstinence society, addressing innumerable meetings, canvassing, and frequently attending at the Police Court to • try to help those who had fallen. Many of the leading supporters having died or removed, it was impossible to continue the work, and though the business of auctioneer and valuer was attempted, yet it did not become a successful one. This was, in part attributable to the strong advccacy of total abstinence which Mr. Winskill never neglected to preach in whatever sphere he was found. An opeoing in the Insurance world caused his removal to Liverpool in 1883 where he had resided:ever since. In that city he had many opportunities to still further promote the principles FO dear to his heart, and was invited to address meetings in many parts of the country. Mr. Winskill was a prolific writer on the question, publishing several books of temperance songs, one of the latter being sung by a vary large 'choir at the Crystal Palace and afterwards taken up in many towns and villages. As a temperance historian it is unlikely that he will have an equal, having published" The comprehensive history of the rise and progress of the Temperance Reformation " (Mackie and Co, 1881), " The Temperance Movement and its workers," 4 volumes i:lustrated with photographs (t3lackle and Son, 1893), " Temperance Standard Bearers of the Nineteenth Century," 2 volumes (Darrah Bros., 1897). Recently failing strength compelled him to live a -very quiet life, and he gradually weakened until Friday of last week when he passed away in his 79th year. He had been a widower for eight years, and now leaves two sons and four daughters to mourn his loss

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The funeral took place very quietly at tbe War- rington Cemetery on Tuesday, the Rev John Yonge 4 fliciating. The chief mourners were :—Miss Winskill (daughter), Liverpool ; Mr P T Winskill (son), Mrs Winskill (daughter-imlaw), Mr Harold Winskill (grandson), Warrington; Mr James L Winskill (son of the deceased), Master Stanley Winskill (grandson), Bootle ; Mr and Mrs J R Charlton (son-in-law and daughter), Miss Charlton (grand- daughter), New Brighton; Mrs W Hardcastle (daughter), Liverpool; b,fr and Mrs Geo. Pipes (son- in-law and daughter), Mr Geo. Pipes (grandson), Miss Hilda Pipes (grandaughter), Bury; and Mrs Adams (niece); Sheffield. Among others present at the cemetery were Mr Ziba Armitage, Mr W Beswick, Mr Robert Cook, Mr William Hayes and Mr Alfred Perris. The funeral arrangements were carried cut by Messrs G Mounfield and Sons. Wreaths were forwarded by the relatives, whose names are men, tiorecl above as well as by Mr and Mrs S W Jeffrey,
OFF HIS CONSCIENCE. SAFEBREAKER'S CONFESSION.

At Manchester Sessions on Monday, Lawrence O'Keefe, a stoker, was sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment for three offences,' two of which he had confessed to the police. In one case the prisoner removed a safe from the counting-house of Messrs. Vaughan and Co. into a field, blowing it open and steal- ing £6. A detective said he believed the confession was due to the man having a desire to get the offences oft his conscience.

The defendant, in giving evidence, said Mr. De Knoop and other gentlemen were in the car and he did not con- sider he was driving at a rpeed dangerous to the public. He did not think there was anything out of the ordinary in the way of traffic on Grand National Day. The car he was in charge of was a 38h.p. Daimler and he could have pulled up in three or four lengths of tho c ,r. lie knew the dangerous corner at Stretton and sounded his horn and slowed up to 15 miles per hour. Mr De Knoop said the defendant never drove the car in a racklers manner. He told the defendant that the policemen were out and that be must be especially ' careful. He did not think they were driving at a speed dangerous to the public. There was a fair amount of traffic on the road hut most of the cther cars were pro- ceeding in the same direction as his Own. There was another car which bad started off with them and it was ahead of them all the way. Mr. Cook : I should like to emphasise that fact. He did not dispute that they were exceeding the limit but his point was that there was net much traffic on the road and therefore there was very little danger. Thomas Smith, stud groom in the employ of Mr , De Knoop, said he was in the car on the day in question He did not understand much about cars but he thought Griffiths seemed to be able to do anything be liked with the car. He had some difficulty in estimating the speed at which they were travelling but he felt very comfortable and did not worry. (Laughter.) He was rather nervous in a car but did not feel in the least afraid on the day in question. The bench retired and on their return the Chairman ' said there appeared to be no evidence that the defendant was driving to the danger of the public and the case would therefore be dismissed.

div.head: MOTOR PROSECUTIONS.
div.p: MOTOR PROSECUTIONS.
Sequel to a Collision near the " Dog and Dart."

Two interesting motor prosecutions were heard at the Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs H C Burder (in the chair), W P Itylands, It C Parr, and W Fletcher Charles Griffiths, Calveley Hall, Calveley,a chauffeur to Mr J Jersey de Knoop, (Conservative Candidate for the Northwich Division) was charged with driving a motor car at a speed dangerous to the public, having regard to all the circumstances of tho case, between Whit ley Church and Stockton Heath on the 29th March. Superintendent 14:nnion conducted the prosecution and Alr George Hatt Cook, Northwich, defended.

The Superintendent explained that the speed at which the defendant's car travelled was ascertained by means of stop watches held by policemen at variot a points on the road. The rate worked out at 30 miles per hoer. There were 57 errs timed and 31 were exceeding the speed limit, but the defendant's car was the only one covering thirty miles per hour. There was a lot of traffic on the road, as it was the date of the Grand National. The distance between Whitley Church and Knight's shop, Stockton Heath, was 4? miles and there were schools on the road. The car passed Wnitley Church at 11.11 and was checked at Stockton Heath at 11.23 P.C. Willings -aid he was stationed at Whitley Church on the day in question, and took the number of the defendant's car at 1114. It was going at a good speed then, and be would estimate it at about 25 to 30 miles per hour. Sergeant White gave evidence as to the time the car passed Stockton Heath. It was going in the direction of Warrington. There was always plenty of traffin in the village at that time in the morning. The car was going very fast. Mr Cook : Why did you rot stop the car if it was going so very fast ?—I did not think it necessary. Mr Cook said the detendant had been driving for ten years and had been in the employ of Mr De Knoop for seven years. F'e had never had his licence endorsed and that was the first offence alleged against him. Ile had had a vett experience and had driven all over the continent. Sir De Knoop would not have employed him if he had been a reckless driver. He had been on that road often and knew it very well. Of course every now and then ore was apt to exceed the limit in the country but it. would have been foolish on the part of the defendant if he had passed a coliceman whilst going at the rate of thirty miles rer hour. He wished to make a point of the tact that neither of the officers stopped the defendant. They did not dispute the times taken by the officers, but when they approached them the car was slowed up.

It would be impossible for Mr Fielding's car to have run into the other and it must have been rice versa. Both the witnesses agreed on the point that after the accident Mr Fielding's car was nearer Latchford and that the hack of his car and the front of the other were damaged. It was perfectly obvious that Grainger's car had run into that of his client. After the accident Grainger's car was pointing towards the Dog and Dirt and therefore he could not have been going in the direction of Lymm. He suggested that when be saw the other ear coming along *Grainger jammed his brake on and caused his car to swerve and crash into the other. Assuming that the police had prosecuted Grainger, he submitted with the greatest confidence that the evidence of Baker alone was sufficient to justify them in convicting him of driving to the dauger of the public. There was no evidence before the Bench that his client endangered anyone. On the contrary the evidecce was that G rainger drove his car to the danger of his client. Abraham Fielding, the defendant,said he was a justice of the peace for Stoke-on-Trent and had had consider- able experience with motors. The car was a two•seater and they had picked a man up and he was seated on the foot-board. div.head: CHESTNUT SUNDAY IN BUSHEY PARK.
div.p: CHESTNUT SUNDAY IN BUSHEY PARK.
A large number of people spent last Sunday in admiring the chestnut blossoms in Bushey Park. From early morning till evening the visitors arrived in thousands. Cyclists lay on the grass, and luncheon

parties camped under the trees. Very seldom have the trees in this famous avenue looked more beautiful. The wonderful mile-long vista was at its best, although the falling petals were whitening -the ground under a few of the trees.

div.head: MR. W.P. RYL6 DS' CAR IN COLLISION
div.p: MR. W.P. RYL6 DS' CAR IN COLLISION

Abraham Fielding, Trentham, Stoke-on-Trent was summoned for driving a motor car to the danger of the public at Grappenhall on the 29th March. Mr Frank Rowlands, Manchester, defended. The Superintendent conducted the case for the police and said that about 11.40 noon on the day in question Mr Fielding's car was going in the direction of War- rington. When near the Dog and Dart Inn, a car belonging to Mr W P itylande, of Lymra, and driven by Christopher Grainger was proceeding in the direction of Lymm from Stockton Heath, and on rounding the corner a collision occurred and the front of the car Grainger was driving was damaged and came in contact with a lorry near by. The wheels of the defendant's car were damaged and one of the tyres, had been torn clean off. Christopher Grainger, the chauffeur, said at the time and date stated he was driving a motor car from Stockton Heath to Lymm and when near the Dog and Dart Inn he applied his brakes and blew his horn, know- ing the corner to be a very dangerous one. Just as he was crossing, another car came up at a great speed and crashed into his Car. He had said to Mr Fielding that if he had kept on his own side the accident would not have happened. The oar Mr Fielding was driving was going like lightning. Mr Rowlands : Could-you not see the other car as you were coming down ?—No, the hedge is very high at this point. When you approached the corner and saw the other car coming across the corner did you jam your brakes on ?—No I had no need to do that. I applied them gently and the car did not swerve. Further examined by Mr Rowlanes, Grainger stated that there was a lurry near the Inn. The other car crashed into them. Mr. Rowlands : If that is the case how do you account for the fact that the front of your car was damaged and the tack tyres of the other car torn oft ? —lt must have dragged on the ground and thus torn the tyre off. Mr. 'Rowlands : What was the position of the motor cora and the lurry after the accident ?—The car driven by Mr Fielding was nearer Latchford. By Mr. Rowlands : I have been warned of the corner by Mr Rylands. The other car struck the lurry which was a good way on the paving stones. Edward Baker, driver for Messrs Fairclongh and Sons. Warrington, said he bad left his horses and lorry outside the Dog and Dart on the 28th March. After he had been in a minute or two he heard a crash and ran out and saw Mr Fielding hanging out of the car holding the steering wheel. Mr Fielding was about 2ft- further on than the lurry on the Latchford side and was just cif the stones. The front of the other car was facing the door of the Dog and Dart. Ihe lurry was damaged by the accident. He had hoard the continual blowing of a horn, and the aound teemed to come from the Kninsford-road.

Mr. Rowlands said that it was with the utmost con- fidence he submitted that the case had not been made out so as to csil for a conviction under Section 1 of the Act. His client had written Mr Rylands the day after the accident and told him that he was responsible for the accident and that he would have to pay for the damage. Mr Rylands had replied that Mr Fielding was responsible and he would look to him for repayment. The sole question was whether his client was driving at a speed dangerous to the public, having regard to all the circumstances of the page. l'he evidence for the prosecution was almost unique. In one's experience of motor car cases since the Act came into operation, he had never come across a case in which a prosecution had been instituted by the police wherein the chile,

The Superintendent : lam not doubting that but would you not expect an experienced dliver to get behind and p•ss another car no matter how fast he was driving ?—lf he had kept his headbbut I could not think he did.

Thomas Smith, 7, Park-street, Fenton, said he was on the footboard of the car and be had a full view of the whole accident. It was a very critical time and if he had not been lame he would have jumped Gff. Undoubtedly the other car ran into theirs. The car he was in could not possibly have run into the other and if Grainger had gone straight on the Lymm-road the accident would not have happened. It was the swerve that did it. He did not know Mr. Fielding and had not seen him before. The magistrates retired and on their return the Chairman said they did not consider there was sufficient evidence to justify them in saying the defendant was driving to the danger of the public. The case would be dismissed.

div.head: RAILWAY PORTER'S LUCKY FIND. -- A Box of Zam-Buk that Stopped the Bleeding and itch of his Plies.
div.p: RAILWAY PORTER'S LUCKY FIND. -- A Box of Zam-Buk that Stopped the Bleeding and itch of his Plies.

To the thousands of silent sufferers from piles the story of Mr. William A. Sturch's splendid cure by Zam-Buk gives new hopes of a happy release from this distressing complaint. Mr. Sturch is a railway porter, and lives at Binton Bridges, Stratford-on-Avon, where he was interviewed by a local reporter. "I suffered dreadfully' from piles for many years," said Mr. Sturch. " The itching, swelling, and terrible pain made me quite miserable. When the piles began to bleed I really thought I should be driven mad. Night after night I was kept awake, and it was only by superhuman efforts that I managed to keep at my work. In fact, I often marvel now how I kept going at all with the everlasting torment of the piles. "I gave a doctor's remedies a good trial without any success, and in addition tried all manner of cheap ointments, salves, cold creams, etc., until I lost all hope of ever being cured. The prospect of never being free from the tormenting piles naturally made me very despondent. " While moving some heavy luggage at the station one day my eye caught a book about Zam-Buk, left in the office by somebody. I read the book, and was so impressed by the many wonderful cures Zam-Buk had worked that I resolved to get a box on my way home. "To my great delight Zam Duk did the trick! It , gave me immediate relief from the tormenting itch ; never had I felt anything so soothing. Perseverance with this rich balm stopped the bleeding and lemened the group of piles, and I began to have some pleasure in life. All soreness was taken away and the painful grow ths dwindled down, until they went altogether. "I shall always bless the day I found that little Zam-Buk book, which was the means of bringing me such a happy release from pain and misery."

W. T. STEAD AS A HUMAN DRHADNOUGHT. Admiral Lord Fist'sr contributes a characteristic appreciation of Mr. W. T Stead to the Memorial Number of the " Review of Reviews." He says : First and foremost he feared God, and he feared none else ! He was indeed a human Dreadnought ! Neat he had an impregnable belief that" Right was Might," and not the other way round ! And so, like David he would march out alone with his sling and stone cock- sure always of plunging the Philistine between the esl l'vgoing alone to a packed meet- einygof his detesters known tester him s and making them all squirm. He hated steams and gasbags and loved to prick a " bubble reputation." Then—no matter who contradicts me-- he was a great Patriot ! I know the fierce rancour of animosity which be roused—a dear friend of mine once wanted to shoot Stead like a mad dog—but Stead was saturated with this treat patriotic. belief that " the British Empire floated on the British Navy, and it floated on nothing else." So in 1885 became to me (like Nicodemus) and told me his Wane, and got five millions sterling for the Navy, which was then in a parlous state. (Ask Lord Esher how he did it—be knows.) Again, when I was First Sea Lord, he had one of his famous interviews with a great foreign personage who said to him : " Don't be frightened." Stead answered : " Oh, no. For every ship you build we'll build two." Yes,‘Stead originated the great 'patriotic deal " two keels to one.', Why ? Because he knew that a naval disaster wee irreparablo, irremediable, eternal. A naval " COlenso " cannot be retrieved. (You can't go round the corner and buy a battleship ,like a pound of sugar).

This week we are having a change of illustration. The above picture is that of an Indian Runner duck. This variety of the duck family stands out as the very best for laying purposes. I have never kept the Indians myself but without actual experience I know of their good qualities and support what has been said about them. I will give you the authority of one of our greatest breeders. Mr. Sutcliffe writing to the " Feathered World " last January says : " This breed, which is rapidly becoming much better known and appreciated, was originally imported, as its name implies, from India to Cumberland. In that and adjoining counties it has been kept since its introduction, about fifty years ago, but it is only during the past ten years that its fame as a marvellcus layer has spread, and now specimens of the breed, more or less pure, may be found in all parts of England. The demand, however, for these birds sprung up so quickly as to cause many crosses to be put on the market as pure. Indian Runners are very active in their habits, and have a running (hence the name) rather than a ' waddling motion in their movements. They are excellent foragers and marvellous layers, but are not suited to confinement, and as table birds in their pure state they cannot be recommended, being small, averaging in weight about four pounds when fully grown, and as table ducklings nearly two pounds less. The flesh is of fine quality and flavour, but their active habits prevent them fattening well. They are hardy and easy to rear, and may be used with advan- tage for crossing with the heavier breeds to improve the laying qualities. A typical specimen of this breed should have a long and narrow body, well elevated in front,and be a sely feathered. The neck should be as long and slender as possible, and white in colour from the bead to about one or two inches from the body.

The head is rather flat, and the eyes are set well up towards the top. The bill is long, and broad at the base, and, as the upper part of the skull and bill form an almost straight line, it gives the head the appearance of a wedge. The bill when the duckling is young is yellow, chang- ing in the first year to a dull green in the duck and a yellowish-green in the drake. The legs are set well back, to compel an erect carriage. In colour the Indian Runner is of a light brown or fawn shade or grey, except that the drake's head is darker, and should be even, and not broken, in the marking. The marking or colour of the breast should cease about half-way between the legs and the point of the breastbone. The wings and shoulders are of the same colour as the breast, and evenly marked, and the flight feathers are white. The top of the head and cheeks should be the same shade as the breast, and should be separated by a white line. There should also be a narrow white line at the base of the bill.

KEEPING DUCKS. Seeing our illustration is that of ducks, a few hints tinder the above heading will be in keeping. Some people imagine that a large expanse of water is neces- sary for Gucks. This is an erroneous idea ; and pro- viding the stock have access to sufficient water to bath in, they are quite content, and do almost as well as when they have free access to a large pond. It ought to be said however, that a good grass run is necessary for stock ducks. Failing a ratural water supply you could easily provide a good rized bath. This could be done by cutting out a good big hole in the earth and having it brick lined and cemented, and if possible, have a current of water running through. When this is done it saves a good deal of time and labour in renewing the bath. A fresh supply of drinking water should always be at band. Never force the ducks to drink foul or tainted water. Once they get used to a regular supply of clean drinking water they will by nature partake of this in preference to the foul water in the bath. I hope that these remarks will be the mean 6of a greater number of duck breeders. I am sure that a good many people have refrained from venturing on ducks for no other reasons than those pointed out.

I have already written on the feeding of ducklings for market purposes this season. What I would like to emphasise whilst on this subject is, that a good many people do not realize that a good profit can be made by duck-keeping. Ducks have many good points to recommend them, especially to the. small- holder and farmer. They are quieter than hens, they do not need much fencing in, and even when they get astray they do very little damage because, of course, they do not scratch like the he ; further they need very little housing accommodation. Just a low wooden hut is all they need in this direction. Ducks are quick growers and good feeders, con- sequently they are soon ready for market. MIEEDS T( KEEP. Like hens—when one cannot afford the accommoda- tion to specalize - a good cross breed serves the purpose best. I will therefore name one or two. A grand laying cross and one that is not despised as a table bird is the Indian Runner—buff Orpington. I might just say in passing that you must not confuse the Orpington with the hens, or ynu might think that n Redcap is suffering from temporary insanity. This is ot 80, since we have now got a very good and useful vai iety of ducks called the buff Orpington ; sFell the buff with a small (b) and you are right.

AYLESBURY- VEX IN. The very best all-round crossbred duck is the above. They make good layers and splendid table birds, and as a pure bred the Aylesbury stands out as the very best. If bred from good stock tbe latter can be ready for market in eight weeks, slid the ducklings should then weigh from ten to twelve pounds the pair.

FEEDING. A good general diet for stock ducks is biscuit meal and crushed oats scalded and dried cif with bran arid thirds, and at night a good feed of wheat or oats. Grit should be supplied and if there is a scarcity of natural insect food a good substitute is bullock's liver boiled and chopped fine.

MISS GREATWOOD'S DUCKS. " Professional duck-keepers like Miss Alice Great- wood, of Maidenhead, find duck-keeping a profitable undertaking. With a pen of four Indian Runners,Miss Greatwood has had three hundred and sixty eggs since the beginning of last October, and is still having eggs from this small number of birds at the rate of three a day. These ducks have a free range of seven acres, and plenty of water, which doubtless; accounts for such good results. Rearing the birds for exhibition purposes is a fascinating feature of the work. The Orford men had little difficulty in beating their opponents and ran out winners by 49 points. The Latchford trundlers only won three games and it is quite safe to sayithat the best team won. One of the finest victories of the match was the one in which Wilkinson (Orford) beat Reid by 13-2 whilst one of the mcst evenly contested games was the one in which Sykes (Latchford) was defeated by Wych by 13-11. The players peeled at the 14ts end with 9 each and victory came to Wych at the nineteenth end. Latchford C, 81; Orford B, 130.
Whitscross F v Latchford A instead of playing on May 25 will play on June Bth. Howley B v St. John's A, instead of playing on Jane 8 will play on May 25th.
INSURANCE AGENTS OUTING.

The agents of the London and Manchester Assurance Co., bad an enjoyable outing on Thursday to Fiddlers Ferry where they were entertained to tea by the Superintendent. A bowling competition bad been arranged and after many interesting rounds had been played the finalists were Jenks and Fenny and the result was a win fur Fenny by 15-8.

In the Lancashire County Championship, Bull's Head, Cemetery and Bylands' Recreation were all successful in the second round, and Warrington again looks like taking a prominent part in the closing contests.

div.head: CRICKET NOTES.
div.p: CRICKET NOTES.

The most unsatisfactory feature of the summer sport is the frequency with which the issue of matches is left undecided. Warrington made another draw on Saturday, their opponents being St. Helens Recreation who entertained them at the glass and pill centre Taking first turn at the wicket, the saints declared their innings at 197 for 6 wickets, leaving Warrington with only an hour's batting. The visitors had succeeded in putting together 88 for 3 wickets when stumps were drawn.

The great feature of the match was the innings of T. Ainge who, going in at the fall of the first wicket, was not out at five o'clock when the closure was applied. His stay at the wicket occupied two hours and a half and realized 111, but the merit of the per- formance is somewhat discounted by the smallness of the ground and the easy nature of the wicket. The fielding of the Warringtonians was rather lax and Ainge was missed on three occa-,ions before he had made 40. His chief hits were sixteen 4's. Bennett was the most effective of the Warrington bowlers, capturing 4 wickets for 51 runs.

Warrington made an inspiriting start with J Callon and W Richardson who batted brilliantly and put on 50 Suns in twenty minutes. With the intro- ducti,,n of Shaw the rate of scoring slackened. W Richardson was the first to leave, being caught at point from a mishit. His. 39 runs were the result of a dashing disphy. T Wright was bowled in trying to pull °Le across to square-leg, whilst Fisher left the same over. Partridge stayed with Callon until f 3 30, when stumps were drawn. J Callon's total reached 33, his play being marked by masterly preeition.

Warrington 2nd. came very near to victory but they also bad to be content with a draw. The St. Helens second contingent were all out for 150, to which the home eleven replied with 144 and a wicket to fall. Bradburn was in excellent form with tbe willow and placed 35 to his credit, while H Partridge did well for his 29. Broome wrought much havoc with the ball.

The Warrington and District League tourney is in full swing and four good matches were fought on Saturday. Warrington Conservatives had little difficulty in disposing of Rylands' Recreation, just doubling the wire men's total (25) and adding an odd run for luck. W Bell was largely responsible for the collapse of the losers, taking five wickets for nine runs. He also carried out his bat with 10 to his account. The Ldividual batting efforts were poor, U Gough and J Duckworth (11 each) being the top scorers for Rylands and the Tories respectively.
Sankey triumphed at the expense of Wilderspool by a majority of 12. Not one player on either side attained double figures.

Walker's Brewery came a cropper against Cairo-street Unitarians who compiled 48, thanks largely to the assistance of D Plinston, who made an excellent 21. The brewery men were dismissed for 33. The Unitarians are beginning well in League cricket.,

Whitecross Recreation and St Helens Cable Company were pretty evenly matched, the wire men securing the points by a margin of 8 runs. C F Maybury headed the victors,' score list with a Capital 14, while T Tweedle batted admirably for his 20 for the Cable Company.
To-day's league matches are : Wilderspool v Orford. Walker's Brewery v Sankey. ‘Varrington Conservatives v Whitecross. St. Helens Cable v Cairo-street.

Thera were many capital friendly matches. Emmanuel Institute inflicted a thorough drubbing on Golborne- street Baptists, T A Knight batting brilliantly for 40. He was the only player to reach double figurer. C Harrison and S Hughes bowled with deldly effect, capturing 4 wickets for 2 runs and 2 wickets for 8 runs respectively.

----- Workingmen's Mission and Orford St. •John's made a draw, the saints being all out for 51, while the Mission had got to their last wicket with 40 on the score sheet. J Smith knocked up a fine 17 for Orford, and J M Carthy (12) did good service for the Mission.

Latchford made a weak show against Altrincham V Iwe best piled on a majority of 60. A Yates est individual display for the winners, so(3e4)s 1 madeya ush while E F Cliffe contributed 10 for Latchford. --- Warrington Secondary School gained a hollow victory at the expense of the Widnes Secondary School, whose combined efforts realized the paltry total of 9. The Warringtonians put together 62, J lt Dewar heading the scores with 11.

Warrington St. Mary's entertained Marston and secured the honours by 12 runs. The winners had the valuable assistance of the Rev Father Mawson vcho took six wickets for nine runs, accounting for the last five wickets for no runs.

Lymm had Manchester Y.M.C.A. for visitors and secured a win by 27 runs. H Shorrock carried off the batting honours with IS, closely followed by H S Saville with IG, and It Wilks with 13. For the Y.M.C.A. Mackie did well for 13.

rappenhall had to eat humble pie at Marbury where the home team put together 113 and dismissed their opponents for a trifle of 33. Rayner was the victors' best batsman with 22, while J Lees bowled with deadly precision.

Winwick Asylum C.C. recorded their third successive victory on Saturday, when they entertained Pennington Mills. J. Farmer knocked eight fours in his total of 40, and G Dawson made 34. W Birchall was the highest scorer for Pennington with 37 to his credit. Dawson took 4 wickets for 21 runs and C Cunningham took 4 for 28. Pennington's most successful bowlers were Winstanley (3 for 19), Birchall (3 for 29) and Gerrard (2 for 13)

The Championship. DRAW FOR FIRST ROUND. Arrangements for the season are now completed and at a Council meeting held at the Pelican Hotel on Tues- day evening, the chief business WWI the draw for the first round of the championship. Mr G 8%11, jun., pre- sided, and the Hon. Treasurer (Mr G F Freeman) and Hon. Secretary (Mr .7 Wood) were also in attendance. The draw for the first round of the championship reeulted as follows :

Senior Conservative Club v Rylands Bros. Penketh Park v Whiteoross. King and Queen v Bull's Head. Liberal Club v Cemetery No. 1. Junior Conservatives v Cemetery No. 2. Fearnhead a bye. The first-named clubs to have the option of the green; games to be played on May 25th and June lat.l A vote of condolence was passed with the family of the late Mr. Geo. Holbrook.

div.head: BREWERY FIRE.
div.p: BREWERY FIRE.

Great excitement was caused about 12 o'clock noon yesterday, when it was discovered that a fire had broken out in the basement of the brewery of Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, Ltd., King-street Brewery. The brigade, in charge of Superintendent Turner, were quickly on the spot and found that they had a severe task in front of them to reach the seat of the outbreak. The hydrants were got to work in the lower part of the building, and copious water pcured on the fire. Mean- while the smoke was very dense and the works' fire brigade which also had their appliances, gave every assistance. The smoke made its way through the general offices and the staff in charge of Mr. Fulton Smith carried out the books and other valuable articles across to the fire station and adjacent , houses. About 12.15 a tongue of flame shot up near the ' door of the offices. This proved to be the only flame seen by the spectators, and the brigade having knocked out the staircase, played on the cellar, where thousands of boxes of beer were stored. 'For an hour or so the brigade did not make much headway, but shortly afterwards a large number of cases were removed from the entrance and after nearly two hours work they got the best of the fight. There were saveral valuable oil-paintings and various silver cups in the building, but these were fortunately saved. A few hundreds of pounds damage was done.

div.head: MARINE STORES ON FIRE.
div.p: MARINE STORES ON FIRE.

Shortly after three o'clock yesterday morning the fire brigade received a call to a marine store warehouse belonging to Mr ft T Harding, of Buttermarket-street. The brigade were soon on the scene and after effecting an entrance discovered that a few bags ot paper and cotton waste were on fire. These were thrown in the street and in a few minutes the tire was extinguished.

To the frequently MR. ASQUITH. repeated charge that AND THE the Welsh Disestablish- WELSH ISSUE. ment Bill is founded on the low motive of cupidity—one Conservative newspaper calls it" the Plunder Bill "—Mr. ASQUITH made the direct answer that he would not himself support any measure to which such an Object could be justly ascribed. This may be said of the supporters of the Bill in general. Who is there in the House of Commons or elsewhere who would give his support to a Bill the sole or the main object of which was to divert from one service to another a matter of £170,000? When this is made the main argument on one side there must be a quite unanswerable case on the other. The PRIME MINISTER agreed whole-heartedly NVith Mr. BALFOUR'S contention that the Church of England is a comprehensive Church, and that it has allowed to its ministers and members the widest possible liberty of opinion and expression. But this, as he pointed out, has nothing to do with the matter. Nobody proposed to interfere with the liberty of the Church in this or in any other respect. The object of the Bill is simply to liberate the Church in Wales from the control of the State. Mr. ASQUITH declined altogether to enter into the question of whether the special recognition by the State of some particular form of religion is or is not in the best interest of the Christian religion. This is something that was settled once for all when the Irish Church was dis- established. The argument on principle was then employed and exhausted, said the PRIME MINISTER. What is now the subject of discussion is the justice of the claim so long and so insistently made by the Welsh people. The question -asked by Mr. BALFOUR on Tuesday as to whether a Church is weakened or strengthened "by being robbed," finds its complete answer in the Irish case. The Pro- testant cause in Ireland has without doubt been gi eatly strengthened by disestablish- ment. For one thing, it has ceased to be the cause of public enmity. For the best part of 200 years, Mr. ASQUITH pointed out,the main energies of the Established Church in Ireland and the Established Church in Wales were not devoted to the spiritual regeneration of the populations for which they existed, but were used by the English Government as political instruments. The result in Ireland was to confirm the 'mass of the Irish people in their allegiance to Roman Catholicism, and in Wales to drive the mass of the people into Nonconformity. The ground thus lost could never be recovered, the PRIME MINISTER maintained, and he laid down the indisput- able postulate that, if an Established Church is to maintain its title, it must be the organised expression of the public life of the community. It has been assumed in the speech of MR. GEORGE HARWOOD on the Liberal side, and in the whole of the speeches from the Opposition benches, that the Estab- lished Church is the essential bulwark of religion in Wales. As the largest and most

active part of the religious life of Wales is be found outside the Establishment, t' an argument that can hardly be put fo: seriously. The effect of disestablishing the Church Ireland was, according to some high auth( ties, to be the extinction of Protestanti, that country. Mr. ASQUITH quoted famous but now ridiculous prophecy of Archbishop of Dublin in 1869. "If," Sal' ARCHBISHOP, "they overthrew the Established Church, Irish Protestants have to choose between apostasy or exP, tion, and every man, when the Church would have to leave the country, or would be handed over to the gibbet or sword." Times deals very unkindly such prognostications as this. The Protestants, said the PRIME MINISTER, laughter occasioned by the memory of incident, is as virile and vocal as ever. speech was a calm and forcible exposition the actual position. The division on second reading of the Bill took place Thursday night, and though there vr few dissentients on the Government side, majority of 81 surpassed the most sa expectations and exceeded that for the reading.

Charles the Second's seizure on the morn- ing following that Sunday at Whitehall which lives in Evelyn's grave prose is well known. William the Third was the victim of an accident just as he had gathered his failing powers for a final struggle with his great enemy. When at the close of her reign Queen Anne was distracted by the violent controversies between Whigs ani Tories she was found one evening standing in front of the clock in the presence-chamber at Kensington. Her alarmed attendant asked what was the matter. The Queen did not answer, but looked at the servant "with death in her face." She was put to bed and died within forty-eight hours.

_ ; * * More than half a century ago, with the single exception of Bright, no one showed such a thorough knowledge of the Irish question, as a whole, as Disraeli. His famous speech in 1844 is historic : " The Irish, in extreme distress, inhabit an island where there is an Established Church which is not their Church, and a territorial aris- tocracy, the richest of whom live in foreign capitals. Thus you have a starving population, an absentee aristocracy, and an alien Church; and, in addition, the weakest executive in the world. That is the Irish Qoestion. Well, then, what would hon. gentlemen say if they were read- ing of a country in that position? They would say at once, The remedy is revolution.' But the Irish cannot have a revolution. And why? Because Ireland is connected with another and more powerful country. Then what is the consequence? The connection with England thus became the cause of the present state of Ireland. If the connection with England prevents a revolution, and a revolution is the only remedy, England logically is in the odious position of being the cause of all the misery of Ireland. What, then, is the duty of an English Minister? To effect by his policy all those changes which a revolution would do by force. That is the Irish Question in its integrity" * * Nothing is ever settled until it is settled right. The protective tariff is all wrong. It is wrong in economics, wrong in morals, and a great corrupter in politics. Therefore the protest against it, and resistance to it, never will cease.—Prof. William G. Sumner,U.S.A. The spirit of Protection is so dangerous and yet so plausible that it forms the most serious obstacle with which advancing' civilization has to contend.—Buckle, _ _

_ The way to mend the bad world is to create the right world. Here is a I.)w political economy plotting to cut the throat of foreign competition, and establish our own; exclud- ing others by force, or making war on them; or by cunning tariffs, giving preference to worse wares of ours. But the real and last- ing victories are those of peace and not of war. The way to conquer the foreign artisan is, not to kill him, but to beat his work.— Emerson.

_ . Protection is legalized " graft." It is an insidious scheme by which favoured bene- ficiaries are permitted to pick.the pockets of the community while the Government holds the victim down and prevents rescue from the outside.—Louis R. Enrich, U.S.A. _

The Protectionist theory appears plain common sense to persons thoroughly ignorant of the subject.—John Stuart Mill. Political Economists have pretty gener- ally agreel that Protection is vicious in theory and harmful in practice."—Theodore Roosevelt.

Progressive Labour League. This League will open its summer campaign on Monday evening next with a mass meeting near Arpley Cannons. The principal speakers will be Mr. J. McVeagh, M.P., and Mr. A. H. Crosfield. Workhouse Inmates Entertained.

on Monday evening the inmates of the Workhouse were entertained by Crosfield's band, who played a choice selection of music in the grounds. The kind- ness of the band in thus trying to cheer the lot of those whose lives must, at best, be colourless and monotonous was highly appreciated.

The Salvation Army. On Monday night the final popular Concert was given by the Corps Band under the leadership of Bandmaster J Lee, when instrumental and vocal items were well rendered. The farewell of Adjutant and Mrs Coutts was keenly felt, and they leave Warrington to take up duties at Northwich. The Band and soldiers gave them a hearty farewell while the main streets were marched through on to the Quarters.

Veteran Oddfellow's Death. Mr. Robert Wright, of Greenway-road, Runcorn,one of the best known Oddfellows in England, died on Monday, aged eighty years. He was born in 1831 at Warrington, and was initiated into the Loyal Olive Lodge in 1853, afterwards joining the Loyal William IV. Lodge at Runcorn. . For forty-three yea! s he acted as treasurer of this lodge, and in that time its funds grew from £3OO to £3,300. In 1800 he was made treasurer of the Runcorn district of the Independent Order of Oddfellows. in 1807 a lodge of past officers was founded, known as the Wright's Pride Lodge, and he was treasurer for forty-five years. He attended eight A.M.C.'s, and was an encyclodtedia of friendly society knowledge. As a Freemason Mr. Wright had been connected with the Ellesmere Lodge, Runcorn, and the Elias Ashmore Lodge, Warrington, for over forty years. He was also a R(.3-al Arch Mason. For more than fifty years he was superin- tendent of the Runcorn Fire Brigade, and when well over seventy figured in the last twenty out of the 670 who competed at the famous Blackpool bowling tournament. LAWN MOWERS ground by special machinery. Send your machines now before the rush.—J. S. GARLAND 51, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Warrington Band of Hope Union. A happy gathering of children who took Fart in the recent May Festival, was held in Cairo Street schoolroom, on Thursday afternoon, when 350 children were provided with a substantial tea, which was admirably served by the lady workers cf the Festival, assisted by a few members of the Committee. After tea an entertainment was given presided over by Mr F Gandy, the proceedings being opened by a pianoforte solo by Mr P Mellor. Recitations were given by Eva Evans, Annie Edwards, Edith Ford, Hilda Kinsey, Martha Peters, Annie Wall; songs by Ada Hamer, Florrie Watson, Percy Bowers, A Hatublett and S Pemberton, the choir also singing some of the Festival chotuses. Mr A Spruce (conductor,) complimented the children on the singing at the Festival, which was most satisfactory. A number :If additional prizes were also given out for ticket selling. The Chairman informed the children that one of the girls, Dnrothy Bowden, who took a prominent part in the performance had died somewhat suddenly and a vote of condolence with the bereaved parents was passed by all the children holding up one hand in silence. The musical items were accompanied on the piano by Miss E Lightfoot.

Ambulance Competition. An ambulance competition was held at Nelson on Saturday for the Wilkinson Memorial Shield. The following teams competed : —Colne, Brierfield,Kendal, Heywood, Horwich, Warrington, Little Ilulton,Burnley and Barrowford. The tests wet ein first aid,stret,cher, individual and theoretical work, and the results were: First and shield, Kendal, 211 6 points; second, Warrington, 1072; third, Brierfield, 197. A member of the Kendal team (No. 3) won the individual prize.

Shortly after two o'clock on Saturday morning a fire broke out on the premises occupied by Messrs. Edelsten, pin manufactuiers, Museum-street. It was discovered by P.O. Dennett, who was in the vicinity of the Police Station at the time, and who telephoned for the Brignde. They promptly put in an appearance in charge of the Superintendent and Deputy Superintendent, and the flames were extinguished in a few minutes, not much- damage having been occasioned. The fire originated in a pile of ashes, &c., near the boiler. The fiiemen had only just returned' from a stack fire on the Cac ster-road, when they were called away to the outbreak in Mussum-street. Street Accident. An accident resulting in serious injury to an old man named William Pollitt, aged 72, of 59, Bewsey- street, occurred in Bewsey-street, about ten o'clock on Saturday morning. A horse attached to a milk float, belonging to Mr. Ernest Wilkinson, farmer, Poole's Plait, Antrobus, took fright and bolted whilst left standing outside the Farmers' Stores. A shaft of the float caught Pollitt, who was knocked down, and a wheel of the vehicle passed over his body. The old man was carried into the Union Offices and was after- wards sent to the Infirmary, where he was attended by Dr. Burt. The horse dashed along until its flight was stopped by the float colliding with the gable end of the Union Offices.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

The most fastidious find nothing to cavil at in the programme at the Hippodrome this week, for the turns are of the high class standard we are used to baying at this popular place of amusement. The Four Alaisanos head the list with their original turn which combines a capital musical entertain- ment and a large amount of comedy, the whole being submitted in a highly pleasing manner. They are decidedly eccentric in the choice of instruments but probab'y the great surprise is felt when they pull a table to pieces and play cornet tunes with the legs, which have instruments inside them. The Maisanos are also very good bell manipulators and on Tuesday night they were not allowed to leave the shge without responding to an encore which was most enthusiastically demanded. The Glazeroff troupe app,ar in a scene entitled " The life and habits of the Cricassians in the mountains of the Caucasus." We cannot verify or otherwise the portrayal from actual experience, but if the turn gives a correct representa- tion of the habits of the Circassians they are a race who are very fond of work whilst at their sports. The whirlwind Russian dancing which is introduced is very acceptable, but the singing at the commencement of the show is the reverse. C. W. Charlton mystifies and amuses with his clever conjur- ing tricks ; the most popular of which being the invitation to any member of the audience to take any wine he chooses out of a small " ineshaubtible

kettle. 11 and Butt are a pleasing pair of comedy artistes, and appear in a new theme "Troubles on the Stage." The house is in a continual roar to the end. Archie Graham is a light comedian of a high order, and was loudly applauded for his efforts. His songs are very catchy, and he sings them in a better voice than is possessed by the average comedian. The Melbens, as comedy artistes, also amuse with their efforts, and Gertie Rex is a popular character comedienne. Harold Baker, described as the real comedian, also adds to the merriment. The pictures, too, are of the usual good qaality.

div.head: MR. F. W. MONKS AND THE WORKINGMAN.
div.p: MR. F. W. MONKS AND THE WORKINGMAN.
PLEA FOR SYMPATHETIC TREATMENT

Speaking at the annual meeting of the East Cheshire Christian Union, held at Brook-street Unitarian Chapel Knutsford, on Saturday, Mr. F. W. Monks referred to the labour unrest. He said they heard much of the unreasonable attitude of the workpeople, but a little incident he came across showed that, at any rate, there were some workmen who took a reasonable view of the situation and assisted their employers. The incident was not in connection with his works at Warrington, but concerned a company in which he was interested, and which employed a thousand men. The manager was one who treated the workpeople as human beings, and the relations were of such a character, that when It became known amongst the workmen that owing to depression in business, existing over many years, the company was not doing well, they held a meeting with the result that they offered to submit to a 'eduction of five per cent. for a period of two years in order to assist the company. (Hear, hear.) They made the reservation that the five per cent, should be deducted only from those men who were earning over a pound a week. This meant a thousand Pounds to the company and largely as a result of the concession of the men the 'company was able to work at full time and keep all the men employed, and they had done so ever since. The difference between working full time and short time amounted in the aggregate to £6,500, and, so by their giving £l,OOO the men had £6,500 more to spend amongst them. One heard so much about the grasping greed of the workingmen that he felt bound to relate that incident. Ile had a great deal of sympathy with the workingmen in the demand they were making, and if employers would only treat their workpeople as the particular company he had mentioned they would not have heard anything like as much of the unrest of labour as they had done within the last few months. He impressed upon those present the duty of backing up any efforts which the minister might make in pro- moting social improvement and the spreading of the liberal religious faith among a larger number of people than had been the case hitherto. They did not altogether appreciate the hardships and sufferings of their forefathers, otherwise they would strive with more sincere efforts to spread the faith they held so dear.

div.head: SCHOOL HYGIENE. Medical Officer on Unsatisfactory Conditions.
div.p: SCHOOL HYGIENE. Medical Officer on Unsatisfactory Conditions.

Dr. J. COOT]: HIBBERT, medical officer of health and school medical officer, has just issued his annual report to the Education Authority on school hygiene. He states :—A recent visit to the public elementary schools in the borough has shown that improvements as to lighting and ventilation have been carried out in one school during the year. The following schools appear to be especially unsati.factory as regards the lighting or ventilation of several of the rooms:—

div.head: Wycliffe; • St. Peter's ; Trinity Infants', Liverpool-road ; Cairo-street; and Christ Chnrch.
div.p: Wycliffe; • St. Peter's ; Trinity Infants', Liverpool-road ; Cairo-street; and Christ Chnrch.

In the Wycliffe, Cairo-street and Christ Church schools, pail closets are in close proximity to the class- room windows. In the Sacred Heart, Wycliffe and Parochial (boys') schools, the playgrounds are unpaved and in an unsatisfactory condition. Thirteen schools are still provided with pail closets. The Medical Officer next touches upon defects in regard to ventilation, lighting, beating, cloak rooms, and cleansing of schoolrooms, which are to be found in the majority of the schools. He points out that the more frequent thorough cleansing of schoolrooms is most essential. It is not only an important safeguard against the spread of infectious disease amongst the children, but it is also an object lesson in cleaoliness which may have lasting effect. Dealing with the work of medical inspection, Dr Flibbert states that 3,091 children were inspected during the year and the parents of 126 1 children (315 per cent. of those examined) were notified by letter of defects found in their children. With regard t‘i nutrition, 143 per cent of the children were above normal, 84 75 were normal and .77 were below normal. Ia arriving at the conclusion as to the nutrition of a child, not only were its height and weight taken into consideration, but also the many other indications of the physical condition of the child. These figures certainly indicate that the nutrition of the children of the Borough is fairly satisfactory. The percentage of children with verminous heads is large, viz :-39 7 per cent.; and the difference between the prevalence of this condition in boys and girls is marked, 14 5 per cent, of the boys being affected and 61'9 per cent, of girls. This condition might be improved if boys had their hair cut short and girls had theth's plaited. Ile provision of a numbered hat peg for , each child, with sufficient space betmen the pegs, is also essential.

A very small proportioa of the children showed marked dirtiness either of the head or the body. This is probably due to a certain amount of preparation of the child, the date of the insinction being known to the parents for at least a fortnight before it actually takes place. A good deal more might be done to keep the clothes of the children in a better state of repair; a needle and thread being all that is required to keep tha aides of a rent together. The stockings of a fair proportion of the children are in rags; this shows a great degree of neglect on the part of the parents. The importance of the children being well shod in boots that do not let in water is not always appreci4ted as it should be.

div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB. Annuirkeports.
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB. Annuirkeports.
The annual meeting of the Warrington Football Club will be held on Thuisday evening next.

SECRETARY'S REPORT. The report of the retiring hon. secretary Mr H Ashton, possesses few features of note as the result of an uneventful season. He mentions that 21 new players were signed on during the season, that indifferent com- bination and want of initiation were responsible for the senior team's poor display, and urges that patience, must be observed in giving the promising junior talent time to mature.

FINANCE—INCREASED REVENUE. Mr Thomas Pemberton;in his financial statement, says : "The accounts for the past season are submitted for your approval. There is a decrease in the membership, the number of members for 1911-12 being 1,313. as against 1,412 the previous season, consisting of 23 life members,l2l honorary members, 1,196 ordinary members The gross gate amounts to £2,571 se. 31, against. £2,140 3s Id last season, an increase of £431 23 2d, due entirely to the first team being more successful in the Northern Union Cup-ties. Owing to postponements, fog,bad weather, Scc., the takings of the League matches with Oldham, Salford, Huddersfield, Coventry, Wigan and Runcorn were very disappointing. Payments to clubs totalled £149 63 6d, against £l2B 4s 2d, an increase of £321. 23 41, leaving a net increase of gate money of £lOO 19s 10d. The bar shows a profit of £B2 12s 6d, compared with £B2 13s 7d. This decrease has been caused by extra expenditure in maintaining two bars. The interest on investments was £9 16s 10d, against £32 133 6d. To meet our liabilities all the investments have had to be realized, and owing to various causes the Railway Stock only pro- duced £268 4s 6d, showing a loss of .£42 7s. Owing to the unfortunate coal strike fares have cost considerably more, the club having to pay full fares on many occasions, and a loss was sustained by guarantee- ing a trip to Normanton, which was badly patronized. Medical charges and insurance to players have been very heavy. A considerable amount of money has been spent in endeavouring to find class players, but without success.

The Works Competition has not been a floancial success, and the balance for disposal after meeting the liabilities will he very small." The chief items of expenditure are :—Payments to, visiting teams, £149 6s 6d ; players, attendants' wages and bonuses. £1,139 IGs 2d ; transfer fees and delegates' expenses, £375 12s 6d ; refreshments, £lO2 Gs Iod ; checkers, £55 Os 3d ' • referee and touch judges, £44 Ils Id ; medical charges, £4B 12s lid ; payment to Injured players, £96 Ss 7d ; officials, £80; rent, rates and taxes, £179 ss. The credit balance at the beginning of the year was £1,592 8s 2d, and after the payment of expenses, including £1,659 8s 5d for the new stand, the amount remaining.to credit is £7O Os Id.

ATTENDANCE OF COMMITTEE. Tbe number of committee meetings held during the year were 62, and the attendances are as follows : H Ashton, 56 ; T Pemberton, 52 ; T Davies, 59 ; T Bunob, 54 ; T Barnes, 57 ; F Barber, 49 ; W Nevins, 47 ; E Osborne, 41; W Hewitt, 56 ; 3 H Wbitham, 59. The nominations for °facers and committee were published in last Saturday's" Examiner."

div.head: LANDLORD AND TENANT.
div.p: LANDLORD AND TENANT.
CURIOUS CASE FROM SANKEY. BUILDER SUED FOR DAMAGES FOR ALLEGED ASSAULT.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Stanger, K.C., Arthurina Lowe, wife of Frank R. Lowe, Mount Pleasant, Liver- pool-road, Great Sankey, claimed £3O from Charles H. Johnstone, builder, Gteat Sankey, as damages for an assault alleged to have been committed by the defen- dant on February 15th while Mr. and Mrs. Lowe were leaving a house in Highfield-avenue, Great Sankey, of which defendant was the owner. Mr. Browne appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. Burgis, barrister (instructed by Mr. T. E. Knowles) represented the defendant. Mr Browne said the alleged assault aas of a 601i0U3 nature. Plaintiff's hushand ass the tenant under an

agreement, of Melrose, IlighfieliA-v-e-au-e-,-a—n-d- p-alciTeWt: to the defendant quarterly. For a considerable period Mr and Mrs Lowe had complained to the defendant about the uninhabitable condition of the house and in consequence they gave him notice to leave. Before the notice expired, however, they found it absolutely impossible to continue to live in the house without seriously endangering the health of the family. They accordingly took another house where they now lived and they were still paying double rent. They arranged to leave Melrose on February 10th, and engaged Messrs Weaver, of Warrington, to rerneve their furniture to Mount Pleasant which was only a short distance a a ay. 'Messrs. Weaver's men were removing the furniture on February 15th and Mrs, Lowe and the charwoman were in the house. They were speaking to a r eighbour in the garden when two of defendant's workmen—a joiner and a painter—came and asked permission to go through the house, giving as their reason that they wanted to see if the premises were in a proper condition. Mrs. Lowe gave permission end later allowed a third workman —a plasterer,who said he had been sent by the "boss"— was allowed to join in the insprction of the house. After they had been there a considerable time, the defendant himself came and walked through the house into the back-room. Mrs. Lowe came out of the kitchen but the defendant walked past her without speaking. She then said "Have you obtained permission to come through the house? " but he did not answer. She asked the question twice more but received no reply. She then said "As you haven't knocked at the door you had better go out, as it is very ungentlemanly to come in and if my husband had been at home he would not have allowed you to come through without permission." Defendant persisted in going through the house, so Mrs Lowe sent the char- woman for the police. Then the defendant asked one of his men to go upstairs. Mrs Lowe told him that the men bad already made a thorough examination of the rooms and that their presence was causing considerable inconvenience. Defendant made no answer and Mrs Lowe, who was standing on the second step of the stairs, refused to allow him to go upstairs, although he then asked for permission. Defendant then said " It's a long time since I touched a woman, but I'll do so now.' He took hold of her left arm, and tried to pull her off the stairs, but she resisted him. He then knocked her down and pushed her, step by step, on her back up the stairs. Eventually he pushed her against the bannister. Mrs Lowe was lying across the stairs and in order to pass her, the defendant placed his foot on her left leg. In a half-fainting condition she staggered out of the house to a neighbour's (Mr Patter's). He went straight to Mr Johnstone and said "Do you think it gentlemanly to assault a lady? It is not manly to do so' and nobody but a cur would do it." The defendant said they intended to do him out of his rent but Mrs Lowe said : "You cannot say that, because we have told all our friends that we were leaving and that we were going to pay two rents at the same time." Mr. Patten said to Mrs. Lowe "Who saw him ill-treat you?" and she replied " Only the joiner "—a statement that was not contradicted by any of the persons present, including the d fendant. Mrs. Lowe's hand was bleed- ing and she was in such pain that the charwoman had to apply ointment to the bruises. She saw the marks of defendant's boot on the plaintiff's dress, and there were scratches on her arms. Although three months had elapsed since the assault was committed, Mrs. Lowe was still being attended by the doctor. She had suffered immense pain. Mrs. Lowe was then called and bore out Mr. Browne's opening statement. She stated that defendant pushed her up the stairs until she was four steps from the top. There were thirteen steps altogether. She was on her back all the time and kept holding on to the bannister rails to save herself. She could not get any foot-hold. Defendant did not hold her by the arm. His body was pushing against her's all the way. Eventually, while she was lying across the stairs, defendant trampled on her left leg and got past her. She took hold of his coat but he dragged it away, tear- ing the skin off her thumb. Mr Burgis : Have you been on friendly terms with the defendant? Plaintiff: Not what you would call friendly—bat I don't make friends with gentlemen. You have had to complain about your house ? Several times. How many ?—I could not count them. Dozens of times ?—I should think so. Every time you have complained, he has told you that the complaints have been perfectly groundless?— Certainly be has not. Further questioned plaintiff said Mr Johnstone had spent nearly a fortnight trying to mend a leakage in the back room. When friends had been in the house they had had to sit with buckets to catch the water that came through the roof. She admitted ordering the defendant out of the house on the date in question. Did you say that if you were a man you would put him out yourself ?—No, I did not. Anything like that ?—No, I told him that if Mr Lowe had been at home he (defendant) would not have come in. Did you feel like putting him out ?—No, I did not. If you had been a man, would you have put him out? —You see I am not a meet and I don't know what I would have done. His Honour : That is a very hypothetical question. Further cross-examined, plaintiff denied that the defendant and a workman named Helsby had already got on the stairs and that she dashed in front of Helsby. I suggest that when the defendant was beginning to go upstairs you seized him by the legs ?—Certainly not. And that all the way upstairs you held his legs to prevent him going up never touched Mr Johnstone's legs at all. And that he held on to the Bannister, and you went up inbatulanaitswtear.y ?—Mr. Johnstone never had his hand on t How did you get up the stairs, to the third step from the top ?—Because the defendant pushed me up. Pushed you all the way up ?—Yes. Where did he get hold of you to push you ?—I can hardly tell you ; but he pushed me. It wee all done in a moment. Do you suggest he was wanting you to go upstairs?— He was trying to get up himself and that was the only way he thought possible. Isn't there room for two to pass on the stairs ?-1 daresay two could pees. I suggest that if he wanted to get upstairs, he would not push you up as well ?—He certainly did so. What part of his body did he push against you ?—I should say it was his legs. You won't agree that he was first up the stairs and you held on to his legs ?—I was on the second step when Mr Johnstone was three or four yards away. Were you in need of belp ?—I certainly was. Why didn't you call to Helsby ?—Because I thought if he had been a man he would have helped me without asking. Did you ever complain that he was not helping you— a defenceless woman ?—No, I did not. I suggest you got up to the top of the stairs holding on to Mr. Johnstone's legs,and that when you got to the top you raised your hand and struck him on t4e head ? —No, I never struck him at all. And that you knocked his cap off ?—No, I certainly did not. Then I suggest that you were going to continue that attack and he took you by the wrists and held you until you were more composed ?—No, he did not. Were there any marks on your wrists ?—Yes. There was one five inches long. Asked what she told the neighbour (Mr Patten) about the defendant's character, plaintiff said : " When he told me what be had heard about Mr Lowe trying to swindle him out of his rent, I said we had heard his character and he should not judge Mr Lowe's character by his own." Mr Burgis : I am going to suggest that you screamed out " You got sacked from your last place for dis- honesty."—NO, I did not say that. Further questioned, Mrs Lowe said Mr Patten said "hush woman ; be quiet" when she put her hand on the defendant's shoulder and asked him to go out. She denied that she had been in a nervous condition some time before the alleged assault, on account of family troubles. She did not take out a Police Court summons for assault, because her solicitors recommended her not to do so. Were you not advised that you could not sumeed ? No. Asked whether she was a teetotaller, plaintiff said she only took intoxicants whoa necessary. Since the accident she had been in each a condition that she had bad to take brandy occasionally. Dr. McKenzie, of Widnes, spoke to examining the plaintiff and finding severe bruises on her arms and legs. She was highly nervous and excited, and her condition pointed to nervous shock. The hearing was adjourned until June 20th.

CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Arthur Moseley, Hill Farm, Antrobus, was charged with having, on April 27th, at Stratton, illtreated a horse by working it while it was in an unfit condition, and Thomas James Moseley was charged with causing it to be worked while ia that condition The horse had a sore on the shoulder but the:excuse of the defendant was that he only used the animal once a day to go on a light journey.—The Bench took a lenient view of the Case and dismissed it on payment of costs.

div.head: LOCAL POLICE PROMOTIONS.
div.p: LOCAL POLICE PROMOTIONS.

During the week three notable promotions have taken place in the Warrington Police Force. Sergeant Stewart has been promoted to the rank of inspector. He is a native of Warrington and joined the force in January, 1896, proving himself to be an energetic and highly efficient police officer. He has frequently been employed on plain clothes duty. He has bees com- plimented and rewarded several times, notably in the case of the arrest of an armed man who was attempt- ing to break into the Co-operative Stores a few years ago. He was appointed warrant officer with the rank of acting sergeant in 1905 and in 1907,0 n the recommenda- tion of the present Chief Constable, he was promoted sergeant. Another new inspector is Sergeant Heap, a native of Manchester who joined the force in 1897 after having served in the Grecadier Guards. He enjoys the distinction of having served in ths Queen's Company of that regiment. Shortly after joining the force be was appointed assistant drill instructor and on the retirement of Chief Inspector Philips he became drill instructor to the force. For several years be was the tallest man in the Warrington Force, but now several of the younger officers exceed him by inches. In 1909 he WRS promoted to the rank of sergeant and shortly afterwards he wrs appointed charge office clerk having carried out the duties ever since. He stands well over six feet and is of corresponding build. The other promotion is that of P.C. Summsrs to the rank of detective. Ile is a native of Hampshire and joined the fnrce in 1910. He has served In the Royal Garrison Artillery, and as a sportsman he is a cricketer 7ith exceptional qualitiea. He is the captain of the Warrington police team.

div.head: WARRINGTOI HORSE PARADE.
div.p: WARRINGTOI HORSE PARADE.

Warrington's twelfth annual horse parade will be held to-day (Saturday) and promises to be a greater success than any of it i predecessors. The entries have reached the splendid total of 153—nearly 50 per cent more than last 3eir. Competitors will assemble at 1 o'clock and proceed in their appointed order to the front of the Town Hall where the judging will take pl„ce. The committee have been fortunate in securing the services of the following gentlemen as judges : Messrs Alfred Asbtcn, Tarporley ; W D Bullock, Altrin- cham ; ii C Burder, Moore ; R F,emminz, London; Captain E W Griffith, Tarporley ; G R Longe, Knots- ford; R B Neilson, Liverpool ; Jas. Tinsley,Daresbury. The Mayor and Mayoress will inspect the procession as it passes in front of the Town Hall, when the diplomas will be presented to winners as they arrive in order.
