div.head: CONCERT AT LATCHFORD.
div.p: CONCERT AT LATCHFORD.

With the object of augmenting the fund for the new piano which is to be used in the Parish Room, Latch- ford, an unusually interesting concert was held in that building on Saturday evening. There was a large attendance and the various items were received with discriminating appreciation. The chief attraction of the evening was the performance of the Toy Symphony (Romberg) and the Toy Symphony (Haydn) by as orchestra made up as follows ;—Nightingales, Mrs Tinsley, Mrs Farrant and Miss Pigot ; cuckoos, Mr Langdale and Miss Molly Fairclough ; quail, Miss,Hep- herd ; bells, Mrs Briggs and Miss W Hepherd ; triangles, Mrs Ainsworth and Miss G Sloane; rattle, Miss Jennie Fairclougla ; trumpets, Miss Marjorie Fairclough and Miss Hutton; druais, Mrs E Atkin and Mr V Dakin ; cymbals, Mr G Ainsworth ; kazoo, Mr E Faircloup; first violins, Miss Marjorie Reynolds and Mr E Atkin ; second violins, Mrs C Gough and Miss G Adams ; double bass, Mr J Reynolds; and at the piano, Miss Mabel Fairclough. Miss Mary Gornall conducted and the performers played well together and thoroughly deserved the applause they received. In her recitation " Stigeland " Miss Broadbent was highly successful and Miss Mabel Fairclough's pianoforte solo Chopin's " Ballad in A flat " was played in musicianly and finished style. Miss Sophie Rylands renderEd "The Rosary" very expressively and Misses Reynolds and Gornall in a duet on the violin " Three Legends " displayed executive powers of a high order. Mrs George Williamson delighted the audience with her two songs " Down in the forest" and "A birthday." An encore was heartily demanded and to this Mrs Williamson admirably responded. Miss Wenefred Hepherd's solo Bach' 1" Solfeggio" was cleverly executed. Mr George Ainsworth was beard to distincradvantage in the ever- popular" Glorious Devon." Miss Mary Gornall dis- played her talent as a pianist in "Remembrance" (Schumann), " Chants Polonaise " (List d'Albert), and Study in G flat" (Chopin) which were given with good taste and fine technical skill. Mr and sirs George Williamson were recalled for a piquant rendering of the duet "I wish I were a tiny bird."

ROYAL COURT THEATRE. "The Silver King." " The Silver King" has been before the public so long that most play-goers have made the acquaintance of that notable personality. The lapse of time, how- ever, does not diminish the popularity cf Henry Arthur Jones' great play and the welcome given to it at the Royal Court Theatre this week is striking testi- mony to its " drawing " powers. Tie great secret of its success is the strong " human" interest of the story and the powerful appeal which it makes to the emotions. Then again, the play is well constructed, the action fairly rapid, and the incidents do not place too great a tax upon one's credulity. The trials of Wilfred Denver,the conscience-stricken fugitive,and his devoted wife never fail to touch a tender chord, while in sharp contrast, excitement is worked to a fine pitch by the exploits of ' The Spider " and his accom— plices. Messrs. Polini and Melford have got together a very strong company and the production goes with a precision and smoothness which betoken a perfect , understanding bets-een the members of the cast—in ' fact the interest is not allowed to lug for a moment. Mr. Arthur 11. Rooke achieves a splendid success as Wilfred Denver,his portrayal gripping by its intensity and showing the true artiste's power to interpret. varying emotions without exaggeration. He is patticularly fine in the opening scare when, after reckless ventures on the race-course, he is filled with remorse at the suffering he is bringing upon others. He also rnAes the most of the trying ordeal in "The Chequers "end the sensational denouement at the Black Drake Wharf. Miss Madge Prenchard is natural yet deeply touching as Nellie Denver, while Mr. Ernest E. Imeson impersonates Daniel Taikes, the faithful retainer, with a breezy whole-heartedness which gives genuine delight. Little Hilda Homewood shows much promise as Cissie Denver; Mr Arthur Wright, as Elijah Coombe, is a particularly wily and plausible" crook ;" Mr II Elliott Ball as the " Spider" is the embodiment of all that is shady and unsctupulcu , and Mr Ralph Leon gives a cheerful and amusing study of Henry Corket. Mr Frank St. Clair is a typical stags detective and the minor parts are all well played. The orchestra, under Mr Tom Boothroyd's conductorship gives a capital programme. including an excellent selection of gems from " The Mourne."

Mr. Howard has been identified with many notable theatrical successes, but " The Lifeguardsman "is acclaimed as his best work. As the title indicates, it has an attractive military setting and there is no lack of incident or excitement. A remarkable spectacular scene—the lifeguardsman's 1,000 mile motor race for a wife —is one of the great features. The play' will be presented by the full London Company from the new Middlesex Theatre, Drury-lane, with Fred Emery as Prince Max and Beth Elliott as Princess Dorine.

div.head: HORSE BREEDERS ACTION.
div.p: A HORSE BREEDERS ACTION.

At the Manchester Assize.' on Monday, a special jury action was begun in which Mr S B Cernley, solicitor and breeder of hackney horses, of the Norbury House Stud, Lincolnshire, sued Mr John Makeague, of the Go'borne Park Stud, Newton-le-Willows (a well-known exhibitor at agricultural shows, including the War- rington Show) for damages alleged to have been caused by negligence in attending to four mares and two foals. There was a counter-claim for the keep of the animals. Mr Tobin, and Mr T C P Gibbons were for the plaintiff, and Mr Taylor, K.C., and Mr Gordon Hevvart for the defendant. The plaintiff said he had been breeding hackney horses for twenty years, and bad won 600 prises, including championship cups. He had exported horses to all parts of the world, and was well known as a judge at shows. When acting as judge at Bury he 15112 so attracted by the look of the defendant's stallion Marlborough that he decided to send some mares to Newton-le-Willows. It was agreed, in consideration of the distance the mares had to travel, that the charge for keeping them should be reduced to ss. a week, and that one of the mares should not be charged for. Ilas four mares, two of them with foal at foot, were sent to Newton at the beginning of May and remained their until July 18th, when they were returned, with no warning other than a telegram sent when the animals were on the railway. The plaintiff saw them as they were leaving the station and had they not been in charge cf his men would not have recognised them as his. They were in an emaci- ated and pitiable condition, and the foals could hardly drag themselves along. He attributed their condition to inenfficiency of food, and decided to call in two veterinary sugeons and two independent breeders to make a report upon them. One of the foals sent to Newton died after its return owing to malnutrition,and another born since July was deformed and not worth rearing. He was claiming a total of £S3O, and had refused to meet defendant's account of £29 for keeping the mares and foals at Newton. The bearing of the case was adjourned. The hearing was concluded on Tuesday. A number of witueteses, veterinary surgeons and breeding experts were called to give evidence as to the condition of the mares when they returned from Golhorne Park. The witnesses called for the plaintiff said the animals seemed to be suffering from malnutrition, and it was suggested that the defendant's rted farm was over- stocked last summer, especially in view of the shortage of herbage caused by the drought. The defendant (Mr Makeague), is his evidence, said he had used Golborne Park as a stud farm for sixteen years, and he had bred a good many hackneys there which had done well in the shows. One of them was Marlborougle, which sold for 2,000 guineas, and another was King's Proctor, which won the suprwee hackney championship (the highest award) for two years, 1911 and 1912. In the summer of 1911 he had between 20 and 30 mares of his own on the farm, together with a number of visiting mares. All were treated together and alike, except that the breeding mares were in different paddocks from the barren mares. Ile had received no complaint about any of the mares except those of the plaintiff. Mr Harry Trowel], the manager of the stud farm at Colborne Park, described how the horses on the farm were tended and fed during the time the plaintiff's mares were there. During May, June, and July of 1911 seventy-six visiting mares were received at the farm. The plaintiff's four mares were treated in exactly the same way as the other mares,and no complaint had been received from any of the owners except the plaintiff. The expert witnesses called for the defendants said the condition of the mares when they returned from Colborne Park was satisfactory, and that the attention which they bad received when uvder the defendant's care was adequate and careful. The jury returned a verdict for the defendant both on the claim and the counterclaim.

WARRINGTON UNDESIRABLES IN TROUBLE AT RUNCORN. "A BEAST IN HUMAN FORIL"

At Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, three melt giving the names of James Monks. lohn Taylor, and John Brown, were charged with loitering with intent to commit a felony in Westfield-road, Roncorn,on May sth The men were remanded a vrisek ago in order that their finger-prints might be takan. Inspector Breese and P.C. Edmoads deposed to arresting the prisoners on Sunday week, following telephone complaints. They wore begging and selling lavender, and their conduct was so bad that the womsn of the neighbourhood all locked their doors, and came te the windows when the police knocked to make inquires. "Brown " used very Lad language when arrested.

Superintendent Ennion said it had been discovered that the men were really Edward Sauce, James White and Fred Davies, of Warrington, and there were 52, 40, and 15 convictions against them respectively for all classes of offences.

The Warrington police described Sauce an a low brute and one of the most worthless lazy fellows imaginable. Ile had fastened like a leech on a married woman who had left her husband, and had compelled her to go on the streets. Twice he had been summoned for living on her immoral earnings, and also for assaulting her. She had tried to abandon her mode of life and go back to her husband, but 66 had prevented her, tie was a beast in human form. The other men were given characters rather better, but bad enough. In sending the prisoners to goal for three mositha each, the Chairman expressed regret that there was no power to detain them in goal permanently for their own welfare and that ef the community.
BLOCK TIN CONCRALED IN CLOTHING. THREE MONTHS FOB BRICKLAYER'S LABOURER.

At the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday before Councillor II Roberts (in the chair) and other magis- trates Arthur Lomax, bricklayer's labourer, Spencer's- yard, was charged with having stolen during the past, nine months a large quantity of block tin, the property of the Firth Co., Ltd.—Mr. W. H .1. Jenkiostinstructad by Messrs. Henry Cireenall and Co., prosecuted, and the prisoner was defended by Mr. te.l. Prisoner pleaded not guilty. Mr Jenkins said that block tin was kept on the premises of the company from week-end to week-end in a molten state. Throughout the night it was kept in liquid form by special baths, and it was suspected that someone had been stealing the tin by pouring it into a mould which bare a special mark at the bottom. To obviate detection the thief covered the stamp in the mould with sand, but two ingots, which were found in the possession of Lomax, still bore signs of the marks, which were not quite obliterated. If Lomax could account for the ingots in an honourable way, the prose- cution would be quite content, but it not he pressed for a substantial conviction. Police ollicera found that someoae had been round the metal bath, and a tin, which had evidently been used to ladel out the metal, was found near a hole in a fence through which the thief had crawled to get on the premises. On Saturday night, May 4th, Inspector Williamson and Sergeant Stewart were in 1,3 thgoes-lane, when they siw Lomax visit the yard of a man named Matthews, a metal dealer, whom he was sorry to say he had had to defend. As the officers approached, Mrs. Matthews very ingeniously asked Lomax " Whica cart will you take ? " The prisoner explained that he desired to hire a hand cart to remove an old wringing machine from his house to sell it to Abe Shaw. He left with the hand cart. The police followed, and when he saw them Lomax ran. Inspector Williamson overtook him and he said he thought a man named ‘Vilcocks was after him. The Inspector went to the house to see Mrs. Lomax, and meanwhile Sergeant Stewart spoke to the prisoner. Tapping his chest he discovered a large ingot of block tin secreted beneath his clothing, and another ingot hidden on his back. The officer asked him to account for the possession of the property, and Lcmax replied, " What can a fellow do when he is out of work ? ' The prisoner told the inspector an extra- ordinary tale about having found the ingots in Alder- lane that morning partly hidden under the root of a tree. That statement was absolutely inc3rrect, for the simple reason that there were no trees in the place. Mr bluetit an engineer employed by the Firth Co., and residing at 58, Ellesmere-road, identified th• two blocks by the marks cast on them from the mould. . .
Corroborative evidence was given Ti Mr Joaeph Simms, forlman at the Firth Co.'s works and the state- ment of Mr Jenkins was borne out by Inspector Williamson and Sergeant .Stavvart..

On oath the prisoner said he had been to Winwick and was returning by way of Alder-lane, when at the bottom of a bank near a brook he saw something bright underneath a sod. Ile turned the sod over and found the two ingots. He left them there, but returned at night, and, hiding them underneath his clothing, called at Matthews' to see if he could sell them. He did not have the time to ask, however, but while there he hired a handcaft to remove an old wringing machine, which he intended to sell to a man named Abe Shaw. Mr. Steel, for the defence, sohmitted that the man had accounted for the poasession of the ingots, and had not stolen them. There was no evidence to prove that he was ever on the premises of the Firth Company. The magistrates held the case proved and prisoner's previous convictions havingi been read out a sentence of three months with hard labour was imposed.

div.head: WORRYING COWS.
div.p: WORRYING COWS.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wed- nesday, two youths named James M'Kean, 99, Bewsey- road, and Albert Bent, 83, Pierpoint-street, were charged with causing unnecessary suffering to threa cows by permitting a dog to worry them. Mr Arthur Browne, who prosecuted on behalf of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, stated that on May Bth two farmers at Burtonwood noticed a dog worrying cows in a field. On proceeding to the spot they raw the defendants with a bull terrier dog. It was chasing the cattle, and one of the cows was in a ditch with the water over its back. Three cows were seriously injured. Each defendant was fined £1 and costs.

MR. JOHN BURNS AND WORKERS' UNREST. The Earl of Derby presided at the annual banquet of the Association of Municipal Corporations held in the Connaught Rooms, London, on Monday evening. Mr. John Burns in replying to the toast of his Majesty's Ministers, said be believed in the idea of fewer ,authorities, but authorities armed with wider powers and greater freedom from central super- •ision being slowly but surely secured. One of the reasons for the present industrial discontent was that the environment of the poorer people had not kept pace with the elevated appetites that forty years of elemen- tary education had created. It was no good to say that industrial unrest was going t 3 be cured by resolutions of municipal corporations, or by some Act of Parlia- ment of a palliative or soporific character. Unrest would continue. Municipal authorities were the largest employers of labour in the country, and It WHS for them so to regularise that employment tlutt the degrading conditions of casual labour should be removed as far as possible. In conclusion Mr. Burns asked the corporations to continue to administer the Town Planning Act in the test way, and to see that they did their part to get the finest results from the Insurance Act.

The Warrington Assleis:ion of Bands, which is responsible for the weekly programme of music in the Park during the summer months, held its annual meet- ing at the Town Hall on Monday evening, under the presidency of Mr. Arthur Down. Mr. J. k DAWSON, hon. secretary, presented the annual report, which stated that during the season thirty-two performances were given in the Park, nineteen on Sundays and thirteen on week-days. The total amount paid to the bands during the year was £96 03 10d, which included the £2O received by the Corporation for the Coronation Day performances. There was a balance at the bank of 3s 91. A new band had been formed at Grappenhall named Grappenhall Subscription Band. He was informed that the members were very enthusiastic and were making good progress. The report was adopted. The Treasurer's report showed that the twelve months commenced with an amount in hand of £5 18s 4d, and closed with a balance of 35 9d. A sum of £7O had been received as a contribution from the Corporation, and £76 0 10d had been paid to bands. The report was also adopted. place in Bank Perk. The work was undertaken from purely unsolfleh motives. It had achieved two objects —to give enjoyment to a vast number of people, and to stimulate and encourage music in the district. He hoped that they might long continue to maintain the traditions of the past, and pursue their career of use- fulness with undiminished vigour. The President next touched upon the effect of industrial unrest upon musical pursuits. It might, he remarked, perhaps be wondered at why he referred to such matters, and what they could have to do with music and the work of the association. They concerned them greatly, and had affected not only the study of music but many other pursuits also. Music was a peaceful art, and could only be pur- sued with advantage when the mind was at rest and undistnrbed by extremes of emotion or the cares of life. Attendances at band practices fell off, and bandemen neglected their home practice, when the nation was passing through troublous times or periods of excite- ment. Probably there was not a bandmaster present who had not had occasion to notice' to a greater or band extent, the effect upon his and of such circum- stances. It was quite easy to criticise, but it was more difficult to suggest a remedy. The only remedy he could suggest was musical enthusiasm. They must practise it themselves and encoura,e• others to do likewise. During the past year he hal worked hard for the two bands which he conducted, and it had been highly gratifying to observe how his efforts had been backed op by the members. Enthusiasm begot enthusiasm. But more than enthusiasm was required. Steady and systematic home practice and study for old and young musicians alike, were necessary,particularly the practice of scales—major, minor and chromatic—and of exercises specially adapted for overcoming technical difficulties, and for acquiring perfect intonation, phrasing, and the multitude of other details which a good musician most knovv. The experienced musician needed that daily practice so as to hold what he had gained, and the young man needed it so as to gain the experience and musical ability uecessary to make him the experienced musician of years to come. He made those remarks in the hope that increased interest •in music might be aroused beyond the confines of the four walls of that room,and that young musicians of to-day might perhaps be made to realise that upon them depended the musical life of the future. MUSIC IN WARRINGTON NEEDED STIRRING CP, and the association had it in its power to do much in that direction. They should, by example and by pre- sent, endeavour to arouse enthusiasm and to encourage boys and young men to take up musical instruments, and to study them in an intelligent and determined manner. Their work should afford them a greater satis- faction than the thought that they might be cresting musicians, in the consciousness that they were doing something to brighten tha lives of many who had little relaxation from care and daily toil, and who had few opportunities for hearing good music elsewhere The re-election of Mr. A. Dawn to the presidency of the AEsociation was proposed by Mr. ARMSTRONG who paid a warm tribute to the interest which Mr. Down , took in the work and said no-one could be better suited for the position. Mr. SMITH seconded, and said in M. Down they had the right man in the right place. The resolution was carried with acclamation. Mr. DOWN in reply said it would always be his endeavour to do what he could for the furtherance of the association. He hoped they might long work together and continue their work of usefulness. The Mayor, Messrs F Monks A Crosfleld, and the members of the Town Hall, Parks, and Bath Committee were re-appointed vice-presidents, with the addition of Mr Ilarold Smith, M.P. The Association expressed its appreciation of the services of Mr Dawson as honorary secretary, and Mr Fairhurst as treasurer and re-appointed them to their respective offices. div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Church.

Preaching at St. John's -Church on Sunday evening the Rev W Reid chose for his text John i. 39, " He Faith unto them corns and ses. 'nay came and saw where He dwelt and abode with liim that day," etc. Christ, said the preacher.' approached men to-day as He did then, asking what their object in life was, not what they might realise but what they sought determined character. As then, so to-day, lie invited men to share His companionship, and to know Him first-band. It was the personility of Carist which drew. Not what, but Whom they believed was of the greatest importance in life, and t') redeem the world they must be able to see where He dwelt to sojourn with Him, and carry Him forth to men.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A.

There was a good meeting on Sunday, presided over by Mr. D. McEachern. Mr. Woolley gave the address upon Irsiah's letter to Nehemiah. Nehemiah, be pointed out, spread the letter before the Lord, and prayed for his life to be spared. The letter slid Set thy house in order, for thou shalt die and not live." The prayer was answered by 13 years of life. Mr. Woolley spoke upon the power of prayer andthe answers to prayer, with some of his own experiences, which made his address very acceptable and interesting. Mr. Thomas sang, " The Holy City "and "The star of Bethlehem " both being very pleasingly rendered. Mr. Payton was at the organ. The Chairman read the lesson and Mr. Woolley led the prayer. The secretary voiced a vote sympathy with Mr. amsharn,of Grappen- hall, in the accident which had befallen him during the week.

div.head: Wesleyanlsm In the Liverpool District.
div.p: Wesleyanlsm In the Liverpool District.

The ministerial members of tht, Liverpool Wesleyan District Synod assembled on Tuesday morning in Greaves Chapel, Lancaster, to the number of about 140. ' The Rev. T. Ga!land Hartley (Preston) preside-% The Rev. T. A. Turney (Liverpool) was chosen secretary. The Secretary reported that there wera 24,847 full members in the district, an increase of 101 ; ssith 2,124 on trial, a decrease of 173; and 5,483 junior member., a decrease of 231. They had transferred to other churches 70 more than they had received. Within the past twelve years the number of ministerial class leaders had doubled. The Secretary looked upon this as a dangerous trend. The Brotherhoods and P.S.A. had lost 577 and 455 respectively. Tnere were ten fewer Wesley Guilds and 597 fewer members. The Rev William Collett (Hoylake) said they had made a great mistake when they broke up their work among young people into sections. They would naver succeed until they had one strong young people's federation.

With this view the synod agreed. On the loss of 176 members by removals to other countries, the Rev Joseph Jackson (Liverpool), said they had great difficulties in transferring emigrants. A great deal of proselytising was taking place by agents of the S.P.C.K. on emigrant ships, and the Committee of Privileges was looking into the matter, and before long greater facilities would be given to Noncon- formist ministers in the way of access to those leaving the country, .

A large part of the afternoon teesion was taken up with an animated discussion of the state of the churches. The Rev F J Pope (Liverpool)'said he fonod men willing to listen to him in the streets on all sorts of subjects but they would not enter the churches. They needed a greet open-air mission. Nearly 200 lay members of the Synod assembled at Lancaster on Wednesday, in addition to the ministers and were welcomed by the Rev W J Chant. Home mission affairs occupied the greater part of the morn- ing session. The income amounted to R.1,998,a decrease of £6l. Foreign missionary affairs were introduced by the Rev T Miller. The income of the district from all sources was £9,503, an increase of £57. The amounts contributed by young people's associations showed an increess of .£l6B. But for special donations the connexional income would have shown a deficiency of .0,000._ .

Out of forty-seven nominations, the following were elected by ballot lay members of the conference to be held in Liverpool next July: Messrs Norval W M.P., Lancaster; Edward Cordwell, J.P.. mayor of Lancaster; II II Posnett, J.P., Runcorn; C W Ashcroft Birkenhead; Miss M'Cullagh, Liverpool ; Messrs J A Mack, Bootle ; S M Hutchinson, J.P., Liverpool; J Rayner Batty, Southport ; S J Bradburn, Liverpool; R Lambert, Liverpool; F T Reynolds, J.P., Mayor of Southport; and E Allen, Liverpool. The synod adopted a resolution as " representing 2G,000 officers and members of the Wesleyan Methodist Church " expressing strong disapproval of the action of the Stat 3 Dep3rtments in sanctioning shooting practices on the Lord's Day, believing that the difficul- ties of the War office in arranging these on other days of the week are not insuperable; also recognising the ill-effect of Sunday shooting upon members of the forces that will on loubtedly lead to greater desecra- tion of the Sabbath. The synod respectfully calls upon the authorities concerned to withdraw such sanction and to forbid the occurrence of shooting practices on the Sabbath Day.

div.head: " Browning's Religious Optimism."
div.p: " Browning's Religious Optimism."

The Rev. Dr. Stanley Mellor preached a Browning np tneinn agr? hiss ei sr msoun C b ea! t baei-strirnog.e,eSt rarichapelno u s Religious nn d ay Optimism." He said Browning was essentially the poet of religious optimism ; he was the poet of faith, faith born of conflict. In this he offered an interesting com- parison with Dante, who was also peculiarly a poet of faith, and whose faith was born of conflict. Not in quite the same way perhaps. Dante's whole personal life was full of cenflint. Browning's was not. Brown- ing's actual personal experience was comparatively free from the harassments of fortune : it, pur- C4BUreodwnoinngt.hoenewohfo lteh oassetecaadu ys e, se vfeonr c obui zee ,r aa,nsds Et against the world and the things of V- e world which were so frequent through Dante's life. Browning was not brought continually into contact with the rough and unkind elements in finite existence. But what the poet might have lacked in actual blood and bone experience, he made up fully in imagination and sympathy ; and here he in full measure possessed just that kind of imagination and sympathy which kept him: closely in touch with what we called the hard realities of this life. Ilia was not a dreamy imagination that carried him far away into some fanciful world beyond the stars ; it was rather the kind of imagination which could translate the soul of its possessor into the inner secrets of the most common and ordinary happenings of a rough and tumble existence. His was not the sympathy which could only become active in the presence of gods and heroes, in easy conditions, woven of unrealities; it was rather the sympathy which could understand and interpret the tears of a little child or the silent repression of a strong man, the smile of happiness over trifles or the agony of grief in catas- trophies. By temperament, again, Browniog was, as he himself said, "ever a fighter," as well and thoroughly acquainted with war and battle in his soul as Dante was in his body. Because by sympathy, temperament and imagination he lived so close to earth and so near to the common heart and life of man, he bel•ame as conscious as ever Dante was of the weakness, the limitation, the evil of our finite state, and the problems and questions of this world knocked as loudly on the door of his heart for an answer as ever ' they did in the case of any man. And his near acquaint- ance with the conflict and struggle of life led bins, as it did Dante, to a new vision of the eternal order where conflict was triumph and struggle wise made whole in victory. Like Dante, be found comfort and peace in the belief in and contemplation of the it-ignite and eternal world whic'a lay beyond and behind the present scene. His was a restless soul that could not be at rest except in God. The vision of the eternal came to Browning naturally in other outlines and other colours than those which were presented to Dante, but in essence the vision was the same. - The very imper-. fection of man here, the very evil and limitation and negative character of the finite order, its shame and sin and wee, demanded the eternal order. It was the broken and the fallen who called upon God and cried for Him. CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
A JAPANESE STORY.

Once upon a time a peasant went to heaven, and the first thing he saw was a long shelf with something very strange upon it. " What is that ?" he asked. "Is it some- thing to make soup of? " (The Japanese are very fond of soup). "No," was the reply, "those are ears. They belonged to persons who, when they lived on earth, heard what they ought to do in order to be good, but they didn't pay any attention to it, so, when they died, their ears came to heaven, but the rest of their bodies could not."
After awhile the peasant saw another shelf with very queer things on it. " What is that ? " he asked again. "Is that something to make soup of? "

"No," he was told, "these are tongues. They once belonged to people in the world who told People how to live and how to do good, but they themselves never did as they told others to do ; so, when they died, their tongues came to heaven but the rest of their bodies could not." THE VALUE OF SILENCE.

An Indian merchant who wished to get rid of an old elephant took it to market. Immediately he arrived, he noticed a man, who, without saying any thing,began to walk around the animal and to examine it most carefully. The merchant began to be alarmed because he was afraid that the man might discover that his elephant was not worth much.

So he took the man aside and whispered to him :—" I see a buyer coming. Don't speak a word until I have sold the animal, and I will give you fifty rupees." The man looked at the merchant and remained quite dumb. After the sale of the elephant, the merchant gave fifty rupees to the silent stranger, saying: "Now I wish that you would tell me how you discovered the injury to his left leg. I thought that I had con- cealed it so skilfully." "I have not found out anything," answered the stranger. "It is the first elephant that I have ever seen, and I wished to know where was the head and where was the tail."

THE ANTI-SUICIDE BUREAU. ANALYSIS OF FIVE YEARS' FIGURES. The report on the fifth year's working of the Anti- Suicide Bureau established by the Salvation Army states that of 4,754 callers at the London office of the Bureau during the five years 2,615, or 55 per cent, gave financial embarrassment or hopeless poverty as the reason for their suicidal tendencies; 45, or 10 per cent, attributed their intention to the effects of drink, drugs, Pnd disease ; 428, or 9 per, cent, gave melancholia proceeding from loneliness and other minim as their reason; 237, or 5 per cent, attributed their suicidal tendencies to crimes; and 999, or 21 per cent, were actuated 14 general causes.

div.head: ANTIQUARIAN CHAPTERS.
div.p: ANTIQUARIAN CHAPTERS.
THE DEPARTED GLORIES OF THE BARBER'S SHOP.

The newspapers have been reporting the annual gathering of the Barbers' Association at which the President, with becoming dignity and touching pathos, lamented the long vanished glories of their ancient guild. It is certainly a long day since the Guild of Barber-Surgeons flourished, and it greatly let down the status of the barbers when the surgeons sfparated from them, yet we hardly expected to find after a good century and a half that the wound on the barber's side is still fresh. Would it give solace to wounded feelings if we told some of the story of ancient grandeur and mentioned a few of the long-lost glories ?

THE FAR PAST. From the humble barber of the past the modern surgeon has evolved. Little as the surgeon may like the reminder it is too true to be left unrecorded. The barber and surgeon were originally one. Getting back earlier still to the Middle Ages we light upon the period when priest, barber and surgeon were one ; and this thrusts us back to a study of the very ancient past of the man who dressed both wounds and hair and practised the delicate art of blood-letting.

div.head: EARLIEST PICTURE OF A
div.p: THE EARLIEST PICTURE OF A

The barber can claim for his calling an unmeasured antiquity. The "barber's razor" of Ezekiel, used for shaving the head as a sign of mourning, is out-distanced in antiquity by the tomb pictures of Egypt which show the practitioner as a smoother- off of both head and face. In Greece twenty-three centuries ago barbering was a common calling, and wounds and hair were dressed with professional skill. And even then the barber's shop was famous as the home of gossip and the resort of the gossipers. In the middle ages surgery got into the hands of the clergy, who through several centuries , attended to the bodies as well as the souls of their flock, but as surgery involved blood shedding it was felt to be out of harmony with the true work of the priest. After much discussion the matter was .taken up by the Council of Tours in 1163,and a decision was arrived at which forbade the letting of blood but allowed the continuance of medicine dispensing,

div.head: TH'E BARBEIL-SURGEONS.
div.p: TH'E BARBEIL-SURGEONS.

The Edict of Tours had the effect of bring- ing a new profession into existence, the noble fraternity of the barber-surgeons who clipped the hair, patched the skin and let out super- fluous blood from the veins of all and sundry. England had its Barber-Surgeons in due course, but like most other peaceable and useful citizens they left few marks upon the Statute Book by which the historian can trace them. In the earliest reference we have been able to find they figure rather badly. It seems that they formed the habit of display- ing blood in their windows to attract the attention of the public and to give advertisement.

This was felt to be an offence against good taste and in 1307 an ordinanco was passed directing the barbers of London to have the blood "privately carried to the Thames under the pain of paying two shillings to the use of the Sheriffs.'

A FAMOUS GUILD. Then came "The Guild of the Barber- Surgeons," an institution which was to last for nearly four centuries and a half. At first its object seems to have been that of bringing together the members for religious observance, and social intercourse, but with the progress of time it grew in importance. Its first master was Richard le Barber who took oath at the Guildhall in 1308 as" Master of the Barbers' Company." The most interesting and valuable relic of the Barber-Surgeons is the large picture by Holbein which represents them being received by Henry VIII. The painting, 10 feet by 9 feet, was the last work the famous artist undertook and it hangs in the Barber- Surgeon's Hall in Monkwell-street,London a fine relic of the departed glories of the Guild. It was in the reign of Henry that dissen- sions began to occur. Surgery was felt by some to be an art demanding skill superior to that required for hair clipping, and the surgeons began to look down upon the mere barbers. The breach widened and the enactment was made that "No person using any shaving or barbery in London shall occupy any surgery, letting of blood, or other matter, except of drawing teeth." But the law could not be enforced. The ' two businesses had been one and were not to be easily separated. Not indeed till 1745 did the surgeons break away to form what after- wards became the Royal College of Surgeons. One bit of influence used by the Barber Surgeons lingers with us still in its results. In 1542 they petitioned that they might be exempt from bearing arms or serving on juries and thus be enabled without hindrance to attend to their professional duties. The request was granted and the doctors, though not the barbers, enjoy the exemption yet. Long hours have always been the bane of

the barber's life, but not every corporation has been so considerate as that of Reading, which issued the edict ; " Ordered that no barber open his shop to shave any man after 10 o'clock a t night from Easter to Michaelmas or 9 o'clock from Michaelmas to Easter, except it be a stranger or any worthy man of the town that hath need ; whoever doeth to the contrary to pay one thousand tiles to the Guildhall."
I,nd this, be it noted, was in. the reign of Henry VI. IN QUEEN ELIZABETH'S DAY.

The great days of the barber's shop fell in the great days of Elizabeth. Then the barber-surgeon was a man of real import- ance. Noble families took t;their lodging in rooms above the barbers'shops:of Fleet-street, and the idle gallants of the day called to have their sword-wounds dressed after the street frays in which they found their pice of excitement. _ _ _

The gittern or guitar lay on the sideboard and the customer took turn in idle twanging until his time came to have his beard starched, his mustachios curled or his love- locks !ironed and tied. The shop itself, if we go by pictures of the period, was more like a museum than a place of business. A stuffed alligator hanging from the ceiling and count- less phials suggested the sorcerer or the chemist, and wax models, rapiers and implements of trade made up a curiously interesting medley. A word picture from Green's "Upstart Courtier" gives a delightful glimpse of the young exquisite of the period corning in for his make-up. This is the routine:
DA.TING FROM 1568.

The courtier sits in the throne-like chair and the barber, after saluting him with a low bow addresses him, "Sir will you have your worship's hair cut after the Italian manner, short and round, and then frounst with the curling irons to make it look like a half-moon in the mist; or like a Spaniard, long at the ears and curled like to the twol ends of an old cast periwig; or will you bel Frenchified with a love-lock down to your shoulders, whereon you may wear your mistress's favour? The English cut is base I and gentlemen scorn it; novelty is dainty. Speak the word, sir, my scissors are ready to execute your worship's will." Two hours are spent in combing and dress- ing the ambrosial locks of the young Apollo. Then the barber's basin is washed with camphor soap. At last the beard is reached, and with another bow the barber asks if his serene worship would wish to have it shaven; "whether he would have his peak cut short and sharp and amiable, like an inamorata or broad pendant like a spade, to be amorous as a lover, or terrible as a warrior solado ; whether he will have his crates cut low like a juniper bush, or his subercles taken away with a razor; if it be his pleasure to have his appendices primed, or his mustachios fostered to turn about his ears like vine tendrils fierce and curling, or cut down to the lips with the Italian lash ?—and with every question a snip of the scissors and a bow." But these manners were for the exquisite alone. .If a poor man entered he was polled for twopence, trimmed round like a cheese and dismissed without a" God speed you." This description was written in 1592 and marks the zenith of the barber's glory. That the description of the fuss made over hair- dressing is hardly exaggerated may be verified from the writings of the Puritans who abhorred such ludicrous vanity. Take a description from Stubbes ; " When you conic to be trimmed they will ask you whether you will be cut to look terrible to your enemy, or amiable to Your friend, grim and stern in countenance, or pleasant and demure ; for they have diverse kinds of cuts for all these purposes, or else they lie ! Besides that, when they come to the cutting of tho hair, what tricking and trimming, what rubbing, what scratching, what combing and clawing, what trickling and toying and all to tame out money you may be sure. "And when they come to washing—oh how gingerly they behave themselves therein ! For then shall your mouth be bossed with the lather or foam that riseth of the balls (for they have their sweet balls wherewith they use to wash) your eyes must be anointed therewith also. Thus this ' tragedy ended, comes the warm clothes to wipe and dry him withall ; next the ears must be pricked, and closed again, artificially forsooth! The hair of the nostrils cut away, and everything done in order, comely to behold. "The last action of the tragedy is the pay- ment of money; and lest these cunning barbers might seem unconscionable in asking much for their pains, they are of such a shameful modesty as they will ask nothing at all, but, standing to the courtesy and liberality of the giver, they will receive all that comes how much soever it be, not giving any again I warrant you; for take a barber with that fault and strike off his head.

"You shall also have your fragrant waters for your face, wherewith you shall be all besprinkled, your musick again and pleasant harmony shall sound in your ears, and all to tickle the same with rare delight, and in the end your cloak shall be brushed and "God be with you gentlemen I" A.M.
To be Continued.

div.head: GREAT INSURANCE ACT,
div.p: THE GREAT INSURANCE ACT,
HOW IT AFFECTS SLUM AREAS AND SWEATED INDUSTRIES.
BY C. A. McCURDY,

_ The National Insurance Act is much more than an Act to provide insurance against sickness and unemployment. Both directly and indirectly it is intended to improve the conditions of life for the industrial popula- tion of this country by not only insuring them against sickness, but by attacking tho causes of industrial sickness, so far as those causes are preventable. For this purpose Insurance Committees aro constituted for every county and county borough. A majo- rity of the members of each committee must be representatives of the insured persons. It will be the duty of these committees to look after the health of the industrial population ; to report on cases of excessive, sickness, and to make inquiry into the causes of such sick- ness where it exists.

If the Insurance Committee comes to the conclusion that sickness is due to the exist- ence of insanitary dwellings, or to improper conditions in factories or workshops affecting the health of the workpeople, they may make a claim upon the owner of the workshop or factory in w hich unhealthy conditions are suspected, or upon the local authority whom they consider to be in default in permitting insanitary dwellings to exist, for payment of the amount of the extra expenditure which has been incurred by reason of the excessive sickness, and if that claim is not admitted, may demand a public inquiry, to be held by the Home Secretary or the Local Govern- ment Board, into the matter, if, as the re- sult of the inquiry, it is proved that the local authority are in default, the bill for exces- sive sickness will be sent in to the local authority, who will have to atiswer to their ratepayers when the bill comes to be met. The local authority, in their turn, may by similar procedure recover the expenditure they have been put to from the owner of in- sanitary dwellings, who may bu the person ultimately responsible for the excessive sick- ness. If the inquiry chows that the sickness is due to insanitary conditions in the work- shop or factory, the owner of the workshop or factory will have to pay the expense in the same way,

The effect of these provisions must be of far- reaching and beneficial effect in improving the conditions of housing for the workpeople of this country. It will be a risky matter to be the owner of inSanitary property now that the cost of an epidemic and the legal costs if a Government inquiry may be the price paid for the privilege of owning such property. It will be an unwelcome addition to the estab- lished charges of a factory working under im- proper conditions to be suddenly called upon to pay the bill for any outbreak of sickness among the employees; and if the Insurance Committee in any locality should for any reason overlook its duty in a matter of this kind, it will be open, on the one hand, to .the National Commissioners, and, on the other hand, to any approved society, however small, whose funds have been subject to the pay- ment of sickness or medical benefits occa- sioned by excessive 'sickness, to themselves demand a Government inquiry as to the true causes of the excesstvu sickness, and to get the burden of payment transferred to the shoulders of those WllO are responsible. It will be the duty of Insurance Committees to keep themselves constantly in touch with all matters affecting the health or sickness of their respective districts, and to furnish them with every information as to the health of the industrial population iii their respective dis- tricts, which the Commissioners may require. The powers conferred upon local authorities in the past by the different Housing Acts and by the great Housing and Town Planning Act of Mr. John Burns are probably sufficient, if firmly applied, to enable local authorities to sweep away all those slum dwellings which disfigure not only our great cities but the by- ways and lanes of the smallest towns and villages in the country. The Act will provide authorities with an incentive to exercise their powers in this respect, which will appeal—if not to the consciences—to the pockets of every ratepayer. What. this will mean to the health of the community is shown by the startling figures contained in Mr. Chiozza Money's Hand• book, " A Nation Insured," showing the ex- pectation of life in a favoured locality such as Hampstead, where slum property is prac- tically unknown, arid an industrial quarter like Southwark. Babies born in Hampstead. on an average, live for fifty years; the Southwark infant will only live for thirty-six. And the effect upon the expectation of life of housing conditions is no less marked when we come to the adult population. At Hampstead the expectation of life for a man of thirty is at thirty-five years, in Southwark twenty-eight. The life and health of MU workers is is national asset, and the Act is intended to re- duce the wastage. The stamping out of pre- ventable disease means a cash saving to the nation, derived not only from the economic value of lives prolonged and sickness spared, but from the enormous cost of medical at- tendance and Poor Law relief .directly attri- butable to eases of sickness which are capable Of prevention. It has been estimated that the cash value to the nation of eradicating con- sumption alone would be not less than £300,000.000.

div.head: Ellie next article of this series will be by Mr. Godfrey. P. Collins, M.P.] PUNISHMENT IN CHESHIRE SCHOOLS
div.p: Ellie next article of this series will be by Mr. Godfrey. P. Collins, M.P.] PUNISHMENT IN CHESHIRE SCHOOLS
Education Committee's New Decision.

A meetiog of the Cheshire County Education Com- mit'ee was held at Crewe on Tuesday. Mr. J. llineh- cliffe (representative of the Teachers' Association) proposed the rescinding of the corporal punishment reaation adopted at the February meeting, that corporal punishment in the schools shall be administered by the head teacher only. Calonel Thorp (Iklacelerfield) said that in the interests of the discipline of the schools he was sorry they had deported from their old regula- tion, and he supported the recension proposal, lie helieved the iutereats of the children were safeguarded in every way under the old regulation. They must trust the teachers to maintain discipline, and must not in any way weaken their authority. Professor Conner said they were all anxious to main- tain discipline in the reboots, but there were com- plaints thtt disciplure under the old syst em was cot obtained in secondary schools. The practice of severe and frequent caning had been abandoned Teachers held ihst c'ass-ciniog did not secure discipline in elementary schools. A great deal of stress had been laid upon what was called the "dignity of the teacher," but he thought teachers were mnkieg a profound mis- take in suggesting that their dignity w-s wrapped up in the power of administering corporal punishment. The most successful teacher was not the one who had recourse to much physical correction. Teachers who relied on the cane were placing themselves in a lower position than if they relied on tfie moral influence which they could exercise. lhe Rev T J Evens said he did not think they should ignore the views in this matter of the largo body of teachers in the cc unty. The Committee had appointed chore teachers, and they shm-ld meet their wishes. The teachers did not want to administer corporal punish- ment. They held that the fact that they had tle puwer to administar such punishment was in itself a deterrent influence.

Mr Alderman W McNeill (Crewe) said they 'should not tahe the pawer of corporal punishment away from the leaden, who we uld exercise their judgment with discretion and not punish unnrcessarily.he did not think their modern education was improving the manners of children generally. (Hear, hear.) That was his opinion derived from Sunday school experience, and he thought that if they Vok away the power of corporal punish- ment they would lower the manners of the scholars. The Cbairrcan (the Rev .7 Grant Bird)said he believed good teachers would produce good discipline. He thought discipline would be best enforced by the head teacher, and that if there was to be punishment it should be administered by the head teacher. That a scholar should be sent to the head teacher to be punished was in it elf a moral punishment. The resolution was rescinded by 17 votes to four. The following resolution was substituted : " That corporal punishment shall be administered by the head teacher or by fully certificated assistant liacherø of three years standing alto may have had such powers delegated to them by the head teacher, with the assent of the managers.

in anotner direction the Act will indirectly benefit the position of employees in sweated and underpaid industries. So long as the law allows an employer the privilege ,of obtaining labour at rates barely sufficient to provide a - living wage, the National Insurance Att pro- vides that he shall pay for the privilege by contributing in some eases the whole, or at any rate a part, of the workman's contribu. tion to the Insurance Fund. If the wages aro at the rate of lees than 9s. a week, the work- man will, at any rate, get all the benefits provided under the Act v.dhout having to pay it farthirg out of his wages to the cyst of providing them. _ _ _

Space does not permit to deal fully with the many indirect ways in which housing re. form and the improvement of. industrial con- di will be stimulated bY the operations of the Act. One point I must refer to. Large sums of money AN ill require invest. merit under the. Act. it is provided that in making those investments the employers shall give preference to stock or bonds issued for • raising capital for housing the working classes. Year by year, we may hope for many years to come, new homes for the people of England .will be built out of the moneys cono tributed to the Insurance Fund. Like mercy which blesses both him that gives and him that takes, the workman's contribution will serve a double purpose It will not only free him front the ever-present' fear of unemploy- ment. arising out of sickness tin the wide class of cases that are covered by the Act, it will, at the 6/I.IIW tone, and without in any way lessening the insurance provided, he used to rebuild a newer and a healthier England.

div.p: _ OUR SERRAL STORY.
CALL itIORTS lINPL/trEDI
in the. house in an underground cellar—or

He paused and darted forward with an ex- clamation to the side of the room where a long, narrow bookcase was. One book, a dirty yellow one, had fallen forward, aud be- hind it the detective's alert eyes had caught The glint of a steel button. In less than a second he had pressed the button, and the inside of the bookcase swung .open, revealing a dark and steep flight of stairs.

Spurred on by excitement Mr..Scafe and :Mark Cardow went down them, while the 'other detective kept outside. When they reached the bottom of the stairs the two men paused. "You are armed, of course, Cardew?" the detective murmured. The other nodded. " Yes—l know the type of man he is; blood is the same as water to Clifford Hawke."

They shuffled on until they came to a long :passage that seemed to terminate in a room ,or cellar. As they peered about, trying to 'pierce the gloom, the detective clutched Car- vlew's arm in a tight grip. 'Look! What's that?—up there in that comer?"

Both men drew out their revolvers and ,dvanced towards the centre of the cellar. 'or all they knew the man who had eluded diem might be waiting till they drew nearer 'before he killed them. A cornered man is a ,desperate man, and unless there was an -underground passage that led out into the ;treet, their quarry must be there. "You had better surrender, Hawke'!" the 'detective said aloud, "there is no use in re- sistance, the house is surrounded, and if you got away you'd be caught in no time !" As he spoke he switched a light from an electric lantern beneath his coat, and as the ,yellow light flooded the cellar both melt ut- tered a cry of amazement. Instead of the man whom they had expected to see, they :found themselves staring into the white, -mocking face of Isobel Frant, who stood in the far corner of the cellar, her white hands clutching her gown from the dirt that lay inches deep on the ground. '

"I suppose you know, Miss Frant, that you ire placing yourself in a very strange posi- tion in aiding and abetting a criminal who is a prisoner of the law?" the detective began sternly. "I must impress upon you to tell all you know concerning Mr. Hawke's. c6cape." Isobel broke into a low laugh. "I only know that I have helped him to get away—that he has escaped, and while you are down here he is getting away further ! He knew you would think lie had come down here into this trap," she went on contemptuously, "but Clifford Hawke is not a fool if his followers are ! You will never catch him—never!" "I see," Mr. Scafe said quietly, "he had a very clever accomplice in you, miss." She laughed. Mr. Scafe bit his lip. It was no use wast- ing time talking to this handsome, defiant creature. He had better hurry upstairs and give fresh and urgent instructions to his men. As he turned away, Isobel's mocking laugh followed him.

"You can't get out the way you came down because the door in the bookcase has a trick catch, and I'm not going to tell you how I came down." Mr. Scafe caught her white arm in ex- asperation. "Be careful, madam!" he rapped savagely, "you are defeating the ends of jus- tice by assisting this man. I command you, in the name of the law, to tell me the way out of this place!" Isobel flung back h 0) head with another low malicious laugh. "Until I am sure that Clifford Hawke has had a good start I will not speak," she said: "Yon are both ray prisoners. It is a case of the biter bit, and I hope ,you will enjoy the novelty of your position !"

div.head: BID FOR A BRIDE
div.p: A BID FOR A BRIDE
BLANCHE EARDLEY, Author of " Kitty Berl —Actress," "The Lady &c.
CHAPTER XXVI!. A DESPERATE COURAGE.

There was a sudden hush in the little room broken only by the quick breathing of the three men, and as she glanced at them Isobel was forced to admit that the one who had the coolest bearing was the accused man. As he, glanced at him curiou6ly, she noticed that while he had been speaking be had stood with loosely clasped hands behind his back, and now she saw his fingers slowly and steal- thily spelling out words in the deaf and dumb language which she alone could cee, as the three men were facing him. As she watched him, she knew that the Gilent message was for her, and she felt a glow of pride that in his hour of desperation he should take it for granted that she would help him, and she fixed her attention feverishly upon hie fingers, fearing lest she lost a word.
"You recognise Mr. Cardcw7" the detec- tive said.

Clifford Hawke shrugged his shoulders. "I knew so many adventurers out West that I really can't say. lam amused, though. at the wonderful array of 'evidence' that you seem to have collected. However, the sooner we gut this over the better," he went on, "but first I should like you to allow me to see this lady, my wife's cousin, out of the house. This is no place for a woman!" "I am afraid I cannot allow yon out of my sight, Mr. Hawke," the detective said, apolo- getically ; "the affair is far too serious, you sec we have taken prisoner the Chinaman Li Yen, and he has confessed everything, in- cluding the place where you hid your daugh- ter Lottie!"

"Poor Li Yen ! He must be terrified," was the amused reply; "these Orientals bare no pluck. I hope,"l he added, "that Lottie is all right. I told Li Yen to take care of her." "She has been taken back to Mrs. flawke," the detective replied, drily, ad- Miring, in spite of himself, the iron nerve of the man, whose self-control never. left him for a second.
"I had better go now, Mr. Hawke," Isobel said quickly ; "don't trouble about me, please, and," she added, "I do hope this dreadful affair will not be as bad as it sounds."
Their fingers, watched by the lynx-eyed de- tective, met in a band clasp, and then Isobel left the room, her tall, graceful figure, fol- lowed by four pairs of masculine eyes. _ _
When the door had closed upon her, Mr. Scare turned to Clifford Hawke.
"Anil now. if you please, Mr. Hawke, I think we need not delay any further. The sooner we get off the better.'

At that moment there was a scream, t4o loud and piercing that instinctively the de- tective and his two companions sprang to the door and looked over the banisters into the lower ball, but as the meream was not re- peated they hurried back into the room where their prisoner wets, the door being wide open. As they entered Mr. Scafc gave a cry of rage. • The room was empty, destitute of that cynical presence that had never seemed quite human. _ _ .

..... "Where is he " he gasped. "Good Lord ! It will mean the loss of years of work if he slip through my fingers ! Fool that I was to outeide " They ran to the sindow, but it had not been touched. Even the faint coating of dust, overlooked by a carelces servant, had not been disturbed, and the sole door in the room was the one through which they had gone themselves, and through which they could not have helped seeing anyone who wetit out. Mr. Scafe turned a white face to his com- panions. "There must have been a trap door or a sliding panel in the room," he said slowly, "yet the houee is modern, and I should hardly think it had 13 uch a thing as a secret exit from a room. He won't be able to get far; I suppose the men are outside?" His felrow detective nodded. "Both back and front are being watched, unless he has an accomplice to distract the men's attention-- He stopped abruptly. The inspector had given a cry of understanding: "That woman, Miss Frant. It was she who screamed," he said. "She stood behind him all the time and must have received some sign from him! That scream was a put up job! Where is she?" "There's no one in 'the house except the footman and the valet," Mark Cardew re- plied, "probably Miss Frant has gone home now that she has played her part of accom- plice. Will you arrest her?" Mr. Scafe ehook his head. "No, we have no evidence really, but you'd better give the signal, Bates, for the cordon to be. donblnd The chances are he in hiding
pOUND. THE Gum EYE—and it I was Mother's. No wonder she was pleased. She had just proved what a blessing Steedman's Powders are to Parents. Nothing else keeps children co fit.

div.head: CHAPTER XXVIII. LOVE'S DAWNING.
div.p: CHAPTER XXVIII. LOVE'S DAWNING.

"And wou really think I dare hope that she will see me, Lady Mary? It is so long now since I have heard anything of her, ex- cept from you, that I am almost afraid lest the sight of me might bring back all the past horror and misery !" Lady Mary gazed with sympathetic eyes at Jaspar Tennant's handsome eyes. They were sitting in the drawing-room of -her riverside house at Teddington, and watching the iilver streak of the Thamot as it flowed past the bottom of the garden. "It was certainly a great shock,'' she said slowly, "but the most merciful thing of all was the motor accident that killed that un- fortunate man and saved her from further disgrace. Poor Stella! 1 sometimes won- dered whether elle would ever shake off the memory of it all. Everything came together, tco. The discovery that little Lottie was really his daughter by your sister,, and then the death of Isobel Frant from 01 overdose of toothache mixture, as the papers called it, but we knew differently." "1 can't help feeling," Jaspar said again, "that I was to blame for all this misery that has been brought upon her. If I had not begun my search for poor Alys' husband that man might not have burdened his soul with so many crimes." "God knows best," Lady Mary said gently. "Out of much evil some good has sprung. The papers of- poor Mr. Steinway telling that last , interview with Clifford Hawke made clear '.poor Lottie's parentage, and she is also a rich young woman as well; and now the whole sad affair is slipping into the oblivion of yesterday. Twelve months is a long time." .

• State • you heard trom Herr • Jaspar assert. " Yes ' • she and Lottie were in Venice when I heard last. They are ,both well." Jaspar frowned and pulled Fifi's ears AS she lay curled up on his knee. Lady Mary was taking care of the dog while Stella was away. "Cardew hears from Lottie very often," ho said slowly. "I think he is only waiting here till she comes hack. He is a good fel- low, though he is much older than littlo Lottie. I think she will he lucky to marry him." _ .
..... Lady Mary laid her hand on his arm. "Patience, Jaspar. patience," she mur- mured, "our luck will come, too, and your happiness as well, boy. Only give time for the wounds to he healed."

.„ A servant crosscd the lawn With an orange- tinted envelope on a. salver. Lady Mary opened it quickly and then handed it to Jas- par, who took it with trembling fingers. It was dated a couple of hours ago, and was handed in at Paris ; "Coming home with Lottie on Wednesday.—Stelln." "There," Lady Mary smiled, "von fiee I was right. You and Mr. eardew had better come and dine on Wednesday ; L shall have her the whole day before you come." And as he went back to the Orel where he was staying Jasp ar Murmured to himse:f "Will she still care, I wonder? Oh, my dearest. I hone so."

Lady Mary was half dozing in an armchair near the drawing-room window. It was ,about ten o'clock, and the moon poured a silver light over the river and lawn, while the soft lap of the water lulled the sleeping senses into a deeper dream. "Oh, Lady Mary," laughed a gay girlish voice, "we nave been looking at you all this time and you never woke. There can't be any magnethim in our glances, can there, Mark?"

The man laughed, and let his hand rest tenderly on the girl's shoulder. "Not in mine, dearest, but there is in yours," he said. "You see I am old, dear," Lady Mary laughed, "and I have not the incentive to keep awake that you younger people have." bottie laughed Shyly. In the past year the g:rt had gained in grace and daintiness, and her pretty, capricious treatment of her sober lover made Lady Mary and Jaspar laugh. The shadow that had blotted the sunshine from Stella's eyes had rested lightly on Lot. tie. and they could not but be glad that she had found a good husband to take the place of the unnatural man who had been her father, and who had plotted even against her young life. As the lovers wandered away again, Lady Mary sighed. "Would her own dearly -loved protégé? find a similar joy?" she wondered. Jo the meantime Stella and- Jasper were sitting side by side in the punt under an overhanging tree. Presently Jaspar spoke, and his voice was. harsh with restrained pas- sion. '
"Stella, darling—l did not mean to ray this now, but I can't wait, my darling. I love you, I love you. Is there any hope for me?"

The girl turned her face to hs, and he. neath tne soft light of the moon it shone with strange new beauty. The paat year of grief and shame was wiped away and it \VFW again the fnoe of the girl whom Fate had led aim to across the unconscious figure of Lottie. "Dear," she whispered, "I have never changed, never, Jaspar; I am yours if you still want me, dearest."
He folded her in his arms. "Want you! I have yearned for you, my darling, and now I have found my parat.lise at ldst."

"We. must tell Aunt Mary," Stella whs. percd presently through her tears; "she will 13.1. so happy." "God bless you!" Jaspar replied. "Ile has given you to me at last !" "Amen !'' she murmured softly, and then once more the lovers' lips met in a long kiss of joy and understanding. Their love: had endured the long, dark way, and now had brotight them into the. broad way of happi. UCH&
THE END.

ANNUAL MEETING.

A fairly suceenful sesson was under Tr view at tl.e annual meeting of the Wallington and District Canine Society, Vl hi ch was held at the Lion hotel on Monday evening. Mr NVaing presided, end there were also preseat :—Messrs 11 Milling, J 'Sanderson, F C Townley ' J Lowe ani J B Wood._ _ _ _

The SECRETARY read a letter from Col. Edelsten, in which he regri teed his inability to be present owing to a business engagement out, of town. Ile hod had great pleasure in holding the (Ince as president of the society, but he was not willing to offer himself fur re-election. Ile enclosed a donation to the society. The CHAIRMAN said they were sorry to hear the decision Col. Edelsten had come to. It would be difficult to 1111 that position, but he wculd ask those present for a nomination. Ile also thought it fitting that a vote of thanks should be passed to their ex-presi- dent for the vain ble services he had rendered and the kindrinss he had shown towards the socs'ety during his presidency. They deeply regretted his severonce from that position, but they we re pleased to know he would still take a deep interest in the society. They heartily thanked him for the donation he had so kiodly sent. Tt e thanks were then accordad Colonel Edelsten on the motion of J SANDERSON, seconded \V LOWE. . .

div.head: WOMEN
div.p: WOMEN

The Prince's Coming of Age.—The Prince of Walea will shortly attain to the dignity of a household of his own. He will complete his eighteenth year on the 23rd of next month, reaching an age which constitutes his legal majority, and the Queen's authority as the appointed Regent in the event of anything happening to the King, will then lapse. The only precedent in modern times in setting up a separate household for the young Prince, is that afforded by the late King Edward. rho Prince and his grandfather have teen the only Princes of Wales for a century and a half, to have borne that title during their minority. When King Edward was a boy of sixteen, he was given White Lodge, Richmend, as a residence, and of those who were appointed members of his household, the only survivor is Lord Mount Edgcumbe, who was one of the «pterries. The Mince is not starting" on his own" qui'ei so early in life, but he will shortly have an adequate establishment provided out of the revenuss of the Duchy of Corneal], and be competent to judge for himself his future occupations end purseets. The Fitz-Roy Family.—The aged Duee of Grafton who will enter his 92u1 year next month, has suffered a double hamavement in the deaths, en the same day, f his eldest eon the Earl of }Aston, and his only Ell viving sister, the widew of the ft at Lord ' nrhyn, who vas some three years older than the Duke. Lord Euston, eho ve:se 61, le ft no family, and the Duke of Oral ton's heir is now his second son, Lord Alfred Fite, Roy. The Drum of Grafton, as all the rid knows, is the descendant of Charles 11. by ' Ilsrbora Villiers, Duchess of Cleveland, . f whom it was said that no one e er heard her carnmsnded for any- thing except her beauty: According to Mr. Phil p W. Sergeant, who has tecorely published a life of the notorious Barbara Villiers, she was ot all the Merry Monarch's favourites the most dissolute, abandoned and depraved. Iler clrreer is one of the romances in history, and the late Lori Euston was involved in a marriage tangle as complicated as anything that ever appeared in fiction. In 1971 he married at Worcester a lady named Walsh, who was connected with a circus. It eubsreprently came out that she had married in 1863 a min muted George Smith, at Glasgow. his man, although supposed to be dad, vv,.s living in 1871, co that it appeared there was 110 lawful Lady Euston. Afterwards it was discovered that George Smith was a married man nt the time he went through the marriage ceremony with Kate Walsh, and this little fe. rgetfieness on his part legalised her subsequent marriage with the late Lord Euston. Iscely Eueton died in 1903. The Cnravanring beason.—May and June are the favourite touring months for the caravancers, n.ost ol whom are artists. The long evenings and tbe fresh beauty of Nature are tempting to those who have a taste to exchange home conventionalities for the freer life "en the road." The majority of caravanners are women. The' perhaps is not strangemeing that they are more tied to home life than men end more liable to fin] it now and again a little ilksorre. Many of the:csrevans carry women only, and hero and them they tray be n et with in the by-roads and lanes, for the screeching and dust-raising motor', which have ruined ordinary enjoy- ment of the country side, have, to a great extent, driven them off the main highways. Every year the Caravan Club has a dinner party, fixed for June 12, and also a meet, which it is expected will be held on the forth- coming occasion at Stratford-on-Avon. May Superstiticns.—The belief that May is an unlucky month for a wedding, is an icheritance from Roman paeftnism but it is cften difficult to understand very exactly whal, old writers bed in mind when they originated sayings and superstitions which have come down to us from the distant past. There is a certain fitness in the emerald being the jewel dedicated to the month of May, but old writers do not assign it that honour because of Its being typical of the verdant beauty of nature in springtime. The saying " cast ne'er a clout till May be out" is generally taken to refer to the calendar meal), but the reference is really to the hawthorn blossom, end the old-time belief that May will not come into bloom until the spring frosts have gone. The Roman ceremony of propitiating the ghosts of the departed took place during May, for which purpose the temples of the gods were closed on certain days, and those who married during the month, dedicated to this observance, were thought to be doomed to early death. Tudor Revivals,—The old saying that " fa lion wears out more apparel than the woman " is no doubt as true as ever it was, but tie dress of to.day is adapted from many tines and modes, and this certainly affords the economically-minded greater opportunities to turn the contents of their wardrobe to the best account. Moreover it enables a woman to select a style which snits her best. In addition to adaptations from the Greek, Louis XVI., the Georgian, the First Eropire,the Directoire, Early and Mid-Victorian, we are likely to see various picturceque features of Elizabeth's time reproduced, in the summer fashions. From the arasts' point of view, the chief fault of the moiern style of dress is that the flgwe looks top-heavy, hagely due to the predilection for large bats. We are not likely to go to the other extreme of Queen Elizabeth's time,but minim—originally an additieu to the farthingale, have already brought back various old-time notions, which are sure to be stilt further encouraged by the Tudor Exhibition, organised by Mrs. George Cornwallis West, at Earl's Court.

, Linen TailorlMacles.—Taffelas is to find a revival in ' linen, both coarse and fine, and coarse shantung will be another cr.mpetitor for favour. 130th materials at ill be emplojed for the severely simple tailor-made, which many women who dress well very sens;bly prefer to the elaborate toilettes to he sees in all our prominent showrooms. The linen suits are t homed with very coarse lace the some shade, crocheted in many cases. Shantung is moro frequently adorned with emboidery of the heavy window blind description. Coarse linens in light tones and shade', are trimmed with dark revers and coil r 4, others in ivory v.hite have trimming in coloured wool embroidery and yet others are decorated with linen fiinge. Fashionable Footwear.—Tho shoe th 3 t has reigned so long es the almost universal footwear of women of all classes, is to be deposed in favour of the high—in some instances—very Ligh boot. The time chosen by fashionmongers for this change is as unreasonable as untimely, for the approach of summer teems scarcely the leit time of year in which to bring hack the boot. Soch however is the dictate of that great autocrat, 1)-me Fashir n, the she who must be obeyed, even at the cost of much personal discomfort. Perhwas every possible v iriety of shoe has been exploited, and for a change nothing remained but a recourse to boots. Or the revival of spats for men's wear may account for the return of the boot at this juncture. Be that as it may, the fact remains that women are wearing boots of patent leather, with various ccloured tops such as aluminium and stidie kid, and white chequered and stepod cloths. The bu' tots which are small and placed close together, are of pearl or gins, in other instances they match the colour of the tops. The Black Satin Shoe.—A novelty is the black satin shoe, with light but good sole and moderate heel. It is certainly more suited to driving than walking. This season's two-hutton shoe can scarcely be characterised as attractive, nor does it add to the beauty of the foot. On the contrary it detracts from it, yet it is accorded a certain amount of favour.
