div.head: Lymm.
div.p: Lymm.

TIIE LATE Ma. W. D. IlutviEu.—The funeral of the late Mr W D hunter of Cherry-lane, took place on Friday last when the remains of the deceased gentle- man were interred in the Lymm Parish Churchyard, the Rector, the Rev G 11 Thurston, officiating. Evidence of the deceased gentleman's popularity was manifest in the large number of mourners present, amongst whom were his father, sisters and a representative of the firm with which he was connected. Numerous and beautiful wreaths were received from relations and friends. Mr Hunter, who was forty years of age, passed away on the 6th inst. After serving as a volunteer in the Boer War he has been in business in Manchester, but resided in Lynam on accaunt of his health. VISIT OF THE C.E.NI.S.—The annual meeting of the Warrington District of the Church of England Mon's Society was held at Lymrn on Saturday last. A service , was held in the Parish Church, and afterwards tea was provided in the Parochial schools. A meeting was subsequently held in the grounds of the Rectory, and the following officers were elezted : Chairman, the Rev %V Bracecamp of Warrington ; hon treasurer, Mr Turton of Latchford ; hon secretary, Mr Jsneway of Stockton Heath. A photograph of those present was taken on the lawn. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Rector for his address and kind reception.

PRIMROSE LEAGT:E.—The annual general meeting of the Lymm Habitation of the Primrose League was held in the Conservative Club on Thursday night. Mrs Legh, of High Legh Hall, the ruling councillor, presided over a good audience. The treasurer's report was very favourable. Mrs Callender read the secretary's annual report. The following officers were elected : Mrs Legh, ruling councillor ; Mr Callender, hon. secretary ; Mrs W P Itylands, hon. treasurer. Refresh- ments were partaken or, after which a lecture on Home Rule was given by Mr W Peter Rylands. Mr E Reynolds, of Massey Hall, Thelwall, supplied sortie excellent limelight views.

div.head: SIR WILLIAM LEVER AND THE LYSIM ESTATE.
div.p: SIR WILLIAM LEVER AND THE LYSIM ESTATE.

The cross-examination of Dr Hodgson, vice-chairman of the Cheshire County Council, occupied the greater portion of the time of the Parliamentary committee considering the Brine Pumping (Cheshire) Bill in the House of Lords on Tuesday. He admitted that the establishment of works outside the salt ares would render the Weaver navigation unnecessary. Mr Hutchinson (for Lever Bros. and the Lymm Estate Company) put questions to show that competi- tion now existed with the Cheshire salt district from Fleet rtood and Middlesborough, but the witness denied that it had any serious effect upon the salt industry of Cheshire. He did not think that Lever Bros. would pay more for the salt use 1 in their industry if the bill passed. As to the Lymm Estate, which belonged to Sir William Lever, he would take it from counsel that there were 425 acres of proved brine land, and that there were brine works there. The estates were 2; mile long on one side, and the bill would prevent any pipe- I line being carried beyond, and thus prevent Sir W Lover being able to make arrangements for the cheapest possible carriage of brine, but be thought the best errangement would be for Sir William to set up alkali works on the Lymm Estate mud use the brine where it was pumped. Farther re-examined, he said the bill had been devised to meet the peculiar circumstanaes of a unique , industry. He could take no exception to the way ' Messrs. Brunner Mond, and Co. carried on their business. They were model employers. Ile believed that with the facilities they now had for cheap carriage cheap brine, &c., they could beat the world. There was !plenty of sound land in the salt area on which Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co. or any other manu- facturers could erect further works. Ile could not understand Sir William Lever's point at all, because his Lymm Estate was on thelShip CanaLand the Bridge- wster Canal passed through the estate, and on the Ship Canal he could get salt from Lymm to Port Sunlight at 3d per ton, when the charge on the Weaver was 101. The other salt manufacturers at Lynam were in favour of the bill. PRIMITIVE METHODIST ANNIVERSARY.

The Primitive Methodist Sunday School celebrated its anniversary on Sunday and Monday last, when Mr G R Trussell of Barton and Manchester was the preacher. At the morning service he took as his text the 7th verse of the Ist chapter of' Ecclesiastes. Speaking of natural rivers he described their progress form source to mouth and then drew parallels in the unfolding of the human life, from childhood to old age. His remarks which were addressed chiefly to the young people, were of great talue to all. In the afternoon he addressed the Children's Service on the story of Naaman, the Syrian, and showed how great an influence even small I kind actions have been in human life, giving as an example the little captive maid's forethought for her master, and how that through her suggestion he was cleansed of his leprosy.— Apart from Mr Trussell's address the programme was supplied by the scholars, whose efforts delighted the crowded audience. The Misses Amy Thorneycroft and Eva Touge gave very clear and expressive readings of portions of the Psalms and New Testament,respectively. Recitations were well delivered by Msjorie Prieatner, Norris Wibberley and James Henry Appleton. The dialogue by Alfred and Lois Priestner entitled "Reasons for not leaving Sunday School" thoroughly deserved the laudatory remarks that have since been made. Miss Elsie Wibberley sweetly sang " Saviour, bless a little child." Amongst the special musical pieces sung by the scholars perhaps Tee master's soldiers " was moat deserving of particular note, the various parts being well sustained and sung with gre tt precision. A pleasing teature in connection with this service was the attendance of many of the scholars of the other Nonconformist Sunday schools in -the village ; this being a sign of the good-will existing amongst the local churches. Another large audierne assembled in the even'ng when Mr Trussell spoke on the subject of "Life through death. " Rev. xxi , 5, " Behold I make all things new." His sermon created a very favourable impression on his audience as be came success; de rm,oungsht r as toerdr wh o awn, d tpharienu—gjhoyfatiluthrer'ough death—life His able illustrations establishing his points in the minds of those present. Miss M J Appleton gave an effective, and in connection with the second lesson appropriate rendering of " Let there be light." On the Monday evening the public tea provided in the schoolroom, and in the capable hands of the lady teachers and church members,vvas well patronised. Thus was folio ed later on by a" Children's evensong" under the presidency of Mr H Champ, who in his opening remarks spoke on the quality and aim of Sunday School work. He said that it should be the desire of all Sunday School workers to develop the best that lay in eat_h individual, uot to remain content, but to press forward, acquit° something and above all honour God. Mr Trussell addressing the teachers and workers spoke of the decline of the senior scholars that was being experienced in nearly every school, and said that many reasons had been put for vard of which he thought pleasure-seeking was the most responsible. "Pleasure- seeking," he said "is not /iron in itself, it is wrong when sought through the wrong channels. Try to give pleasure to ot'iers and you will also obtain it.' Aft-r enumerating the various improvements that people advised he said that the chief way was to teach the example of Christ more. Sunday school workers had only a very small perJentage of time in a year, roughly 24 hours per annum in all, all they mist there- fore make t'lle very best use of that short period in which to fir in the minis of the scholars the funia- mantels of God's gift to the world as told in John 3, 16 They must visualise Jean; of Nazareth, show His humanity, trials, and love. Ile appealed to the teachers to become living examples and to do their beet for.the Sunday rchool work. The ltev. H. W. B. Whiteway also spoke for a few minutes on ono of the points mentioned by Mr Trussell, namely that of the minute period of time the teachers have at their disposal in which to instil Christian truths into their scholars' minis, and he impressed upon the parents present the fact that it largely rests upon them as to what their children become. . .

... Recitations were very creditably given by the Misses Bessie Cross, Annie Rowles, and Mollie Tonge. Little Norman Holt supplied a delightful solo, "A child's evening prayer," which won for him the approval of all

present. The offertories were all taken up by the appointed scholars. Special concerted pieces were sung with marked effect by the scholars at each of the services and fully merited the chairman's eulogistic praise, which was endorsed by the many people who have heard them, and should be gratifying to Mr J Edwards, the conductor, and Miss Shore, the organist. The financial results of the anniversary have a'so topped the record.

div.head: DISTRICT fiE
div.p: DISTRICT fiE
Lymm Petty Sessions.

WIDNIMAX.—Before Messrs A Watkin (in the OAP 3 E G Grove., T J Ridgway and the Hon. J E Cross. IVING WITHOCT A LICENCE.—MabeI Meals, Newfield House, Lymrn, was summoned for driving a motor car without having a dliver's licence in the Warrington-road, Agden on the 7th May. The defendant admitted the cffence and said she had only charge of the steering wheel for five minutes and was receiving driving instructions from her chauffeur She took out a licence the next day. Evidence was given by her brother-in-law to the effect that he had told her to receive instructions from the driver and he also

explained that in London the police did not take action whilst the persons were receiving instructions. The case was dismissed on payment of costs, the magistrates remarking that there was no intention to break the law BICYCLE OFFENCES,—For riding bicycles on the footpath on the 18th April, Samuel Andrews, joiner, 75, Stamford Park-road, Altrincham, John Thomson, joiner, 10, York-road, Bowdon, Alfred Oxley, labourer, 29, Chapel-street, Altrincham, were fined 2s. 61. each. William Marsh, Swineyard Hall, lligh Legh, add Herbert Rigby, Rush Green, Lymna, were each fined 53. for riding bicycles without lights. JUVENILE THEFT Casx.—William Kettle (15), 7, Williams-square, Northwich, was charged with stealing a 41b. box of toffee value Is. 9d.and a tin of coffee value 3d., the property of Alexandra Davies, from his shop counter at Heatley, Lymm, on the Bth May.—Kettle pleeded guilty and was bound over for six months. HATH CHARMS ?—George Cooke, 86, Orford- lane, Warrington, was summoned for playing a street organ within 100 yards of a dwelling-house at Booth's Hill, Lymm, on April 27th, to the annoyance of the inmates after being requested to desist by Sergeant Washington.—Cooke was also summoned for permitting a steam organ to be played to the annoyance of resi- dents in Booth's Hill on April 29th.—Sergeant Washing- ton said on the date in question he saw the defendant who was a roundabout proprietor, and told him he had been requested to ask him to desist from playing an organ. Defendant replied : " Oh, no ! I shall go on with the music," and continued playing.—A resident in the district said he requested the sergeant to warn the defendant to stop the organ, as his mother was unwell. —Sergeant Knott said on April 29th he heard the steam organ playing.—James Struthers also gave evidence as to the organ being played by eteam.—William Kettle, of Northwich, said he was employed by the defendant to look after the round. shouts. The organ was being played both by steam and hand on April 29t1.1.—Defendmt denied that the organ I was played by steam on April 29th.—A fine of Sc including costs was imposed in the first case and ss. and costs in the second.

div.head: Mother and Vaccination. CAN SHE LEGALFX Cf.AIM EXEMPTION? INTERESTING POINT RAISED AT THE SESSIONS.
div.p: Mother and Vaccination. CAN SHE LEGALFX Cf.AIM EXEMPTION? INTERESTING POINT RAISED AT THE SESSIONS.

_ At the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday an interesting case heard was the one in which Mr Mercer, relieving officer to the Bucklow Union, applied for a vaccination order to be made against Edward Blackburn, Ileathlands, Moss Brow, Warburton. under section 31 of the Vaccination Act of 1867, in respect of his child Arthur. Mr T S Steel (Warrington), said he was instructed to appear on behalf of the Bucklow Borrtd of Guardians for the relieving officer of the district. Ile understood the case had been before the magistrates a 'month ago, when a question arose as to a declaration of exemption made by the defendant's wife and the case was adjourned. Tha defendant was a machine driller. rhe child was born on the 11th September 1911. Those proceeding were not being taken with a view to having a penalty inflicted but he asked for an order for the child to be vaccinated. When the child was born the defendant went to see Mr Merrier, the registrar of births, and he was handed "form A" requiring the child to be vaccinated. On that form was a form of declaration of exemption, so that if the parent of the child desired to apply for exemption from vaccination he must fill up that form within four months from the birth of the child and it must be delivered to the vaccination cffieer within seven days after that. On the 19th December Mr Mercer not having received the declaration sent "form Q, " giving notice that the child would be four months old on a certain day and unless he received within seven days from that day a certificate of successful vaccination or the form of exemption it would be necessary to take action under the Vaccination Act. On January 6th a declaration of exemption was made by the wife. That declaration, however, was net binding. The next day Mr Mercer wrote the defendant to the effect that that declaration did not exempt the child from vaccination, as it should have been made by the father. He enclosed a form of declaration, and the defendant had then four days in which he could have merle the declaration. He, however, did not make the declaration until the 13th January and that was two days over tho time allowed by Parliament. On the following Sunday this was received by Mr Mercer cud he wrote to the defendant to the effect that it was necessary for him to have the child vaccinated because he had not sent the declaration before and be (Mr Mercer) would be glad to receive a certificate of successful vaccination. The public, vaccinator called to operate on the child on the sth January but he was refused permission. Mr Mercer called afterwards, but the defendant was not at home, so the summons was issued. He (Mr Seeel) understood the question that arose was the question as to whether the declaration made by the mother was within the meaning of the Act. Bythe law of the country the father was the one entitled above everyone else to the custody of the child. The Clerk : I am not with you in that. Mr Steel, continu ing,said that the father was entitled except in certain circumstancee. In 1893 an Act of Parliament was passed permitting a parent or other person having custody of the child to obtain exemption from the Act of 1867. In 1938 the Act was amended to the effect that a parent or other person having the custody of the child could obtain a declaration of exemption, but instead of making it necessary to make the parent satisfy two justices, it gave him the oppor- tunity of making a declaration before one justice or a commissioner for oaths. In the present case the father and mother were living together and he contended that the father under such circumstances was the parent and that the provision in the form of "parent, or other person having the custody 'applied only where the father was dead and the mother had the custody of the child. Then the other alternative Cams that if the father and mother were dead the other person having the custody of the child was respensible. It was always the father, if be were living, who made the declaration of exemption. What he held was that in the present case the father was the parent and the sole person responsible for the declaration and that the wife would have been responsible if he had been deal. Thera had been no decision on the matter in the High Courts, but he quoted several opiniens of eminent men who coincided with his view. The defendant could not plead ignorance because he had had a declaration of exemption for another child. The chairman : The whole thing is the bad drafting of the Bill. Mr. Steel : Yes. Mr Mercer supported Mr Steel's statements in evidence. The defendant said he was very busy at the time and he thought it weuld be all right if his wife filled in the form. They both objected to vaccination. The magistrates retired and on their return the Chairman said that after considering rag the circum- stances of the case and the uncertainty as to the mean- ing of the word "parent" at the head of Form "A," the Bench were unanimously of the opinion that no order should be made in that case.
Mr Steel: Could you state a case? The Chsirman : You have our decision and you know the remedy. Mr. Steel : Yes, but I shoulcj, have liked you to state a case.
INDUSTRIAL INSURANCE COMPANIES. AMALGAMATION TO FORM AN APPROVED SOCIETY. .

Some of theleading industrial insurance institutions including the Refuge, Pearl, Brittonic and London and Manchester Insurance Companies, have decided to amalgsmste for the purpose of forming an approved society to work the Insurance Act. The combination whose policy holders run into many millions,will possess the largest 'limber of agents of any insuLance concern in the kingdom. The chairman of the association is Mr F T Jefferson, Birmingham, the chairman of the Britannic Insurance Company.

div.head: ,RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: ,RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL. ,HIGh DEATH-RATE DEPLORED. In tlie absence of the Islnyor (Alderman F Neil), Councillor T Smith (deputy mayor) presided over the ‘Vidnes Town Council on Tuesday. Councilor Garghan, commenting on the Highway Committee's minutes raid the Corporation had had a lot of trouble recently with the 'buses. Criticising the management, he said the time had come for a special committee to make inquiries. On the wage list he was informed that a servant in the Corporation's employ, who was in receipt of a salary of £2 10s per week, had been employed on extra duty of forty-one hours at a charge of is per hour. At that time a lot of conductors and others were idle owing to breakdowns, and he suggested that they could have done the work equally as well. _ .

Councillor Clarke replied that the Council had throttled the committee when they only gave them four buses. The demand had been so great, overcrowding resulted, and, as a consequence the buses were in a tad state.

div.head: UNICIPAL NURSE _NEEDED
div.p: UNICIPAL NURSE _NEEDED

Councillor Crawford, during the discussion on the health minutes, deplored the high death-rate, chiefly infantile. He suggested that it would be wise to appoint a nurse to go round and instruct mothers upon the feeding and cire of the young.

div.head: COAL STRIE-E EC-110E3,
div.p: COAL STRIE-E EC-110E3,

Alderman Timmis referred the Council to the engineer's report on the gas and water minutes. The total cost of the strike to both departments was esti- mated at £3,.(i I. In connection with the coke sales during the strike period, the number of cash sales for small quantities reached the large figure of 11,220. In ordinary times the total hovers about 1,100. One of the great lessons learned from the strike was the provision of a much greater coal storage, and a scheme for this purpose was under discussion. Councillor Beecham deprecated this i3ea. With the advent of electricity in the town, and the possibility of a strike riot not coming again for twcnty years, the matter could be left in abeyance.

081 ECTION TO AN APPOINTMENT. The Education Committee's minutes created much discussion, and Alderman G Neil moved, and Coun- cillor. Clarke seconded, that the whole of the minutes be referred back. The alderman took exception to the recommendation that Mrs. Corns, be appointed bead mistress of the junior department at a beginning salary of £l3O. It was contended that Mrs Corns was an old servant and would ret,re in four years' time. Modern methods were necessary, aud the position ought tojhave been open for a younger teacher Upon a vote being taken the original minutes were passed by 10 votes to 7.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
MR. J. A. SEDDON AND TOM MANN'S SENTENCE.

Mr. J. A. Seddon, Labour candidate for the Newton Division, addressed a series of meetings in Ashton-in- Makerfield on Saturday. He said that the recent labour struggles had aroused the opposition of the labouring class, and they had begun to use the power they possessed through the courts of law, which were supposed to be based upon equity, and justice. A few months ago there was a little upset at Earlestown, and some windows were broken, with the result that four men were arrested. They were con- victed because two policemen swore they had seen them do certain things, whereas there were a thousand who could swear to the contrary. Then there was the prose- cution of Tom Mann and other people, who had said that the soldiers of this country were not paid to shoot men down when they were striking for their rights. They said they believed the Army of this country was to defend the country against a foreign foe and they asked the soldiers, when there was a disturbance and when the working men were standing up for their rights, not to shoot them down. (Hear, hear.) Tom Mann preached that: doctrine, and he would preach the same. (Applause.) It was a gross abuse of the powers of the Army to get the soldiery to come out in defence of private property and shoot down men who were standing up for their rights. Tom Mann did what every Britisher was morally bound to do—he asked the soldiers not to shoot their brothers when they were asking for a living wage, for the soldier came from the working clam For that he gut six months. If they were going to allow a man to be sent to prison for standing up for tie rights of the workers, they were little removed from serfdom, and they were not the free men they claimed to be. The Government had made a huge blunder, because Tom Mann had only stood up for the right of free speech, and they must demand his release at. the first possible moment. (Applause).

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
YEARLY EXHIBITION OPENED.

The thirteenth yearly exhibition of water-colour drawings and oil-paintings, the work of the members of the St. Helena Sketching Club was opened on Tuesday at the club-rooms, Ormskirk-street. It includes 150 pictures, many of which are worthy qf great attention. The club this year appeals for wider support and an increased membership. Mr Thomas Ellison, R C.A., has eighteen exhibits, which include subjects of groat artistic feeling. Mr Ralph W Bardill, has also more than a local reputation for beautifully executed paintings of North Wales scenery and South country pastorale. His " Shepherd's Crag " was hung in the last Liverpool autumn exhibition, and like Mr Ellison, his work gives distinct evidences of progress and really intelligent grasp. Mr Divid Hewitt has thirteen oil paintings on view. His mountaineering subjects are boldly and successfully treated, "On the Glyders" being especially clever. Mr II J Lion contributes several capital I sketches of Wharfedale sosnes,and his Eccleston studies command much attention. Works ot much artistio merit are also shown by Mr R Seddon, Mr Hamilton, 1 Koarne, Mrs Emily J Skeaping, Miss Bates, Mr .1 Skeaping, Miss I R Bold, Miss Dutton, Mrs. Hyde, Ms Dearnley, Mr Jacobs, Mr Hush Penman, Mr J N Kelly, Mif S Slinger, Miss Birchall, Mr Geo Hewitt and other members. Mr. Hamilton Kearne presided at the opening, when theclubrooms were crowded. Alderman Dixon Nuttall (the president of the club), in declaring the exhibition open, said the members had worked for many years to keep art alive in the town, and were worthy of the beet support they could give. Ho thought that was the best exhibition from the point of quality of work they had ever held. - -

div.head: MONEY-LENDING DISPUTE. ---- WARRINGTON AUCTIONEER'S CLAIM. -- Baseless Allegation of Trickery.
div.p: MONEY-LENDING DISPUTE. ---- WARRINGTON AUCTIONEER'S CLAIM. -- Baseless Allegation of Trickery.

A singular case was heard at the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Stanger, K.C., when John Mainwaring, auctioneer, Warrington, sued Henry Houghton, of Egremont, for £4l 16s 4d, alleged to be due on promissory notes. Mr Sydney Wellhead (Messrs Spencer Wellhead and Son) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr Lies, barrister (instructed by Mr Gaskin, of Liverpool) represented the defendant. Plaintiff's case was that on several occasions he had lent money to the defendant and that about nine years ago there was a balance of £6l lOs due on a promissory note. The defendant called his creditors together and a number of them accepted a composition by which they received 4s 3d in the L. Plaintiff did not sign an ncoeptance of that composition but he received his proportion—l 4 10s—thus reducing his account to £5O. After that time there were no transactions between the parties for some years but plaintiff, in k x plaini g why be did not press for pay- ment of the balance, said he knew defendant's father was very well off and he felt sure he would ultimately be paid. As a matter of fact it was alleged that defendant came into an income of £6OO a year. The old debt became barred by the statute of limitations in 1903, but in April, 1910, defendant borrowed a further £3 153 on promissory note and at the same time signed an undertaking : "I hereby undertake to pay off the whole of my indebtedness to you on or before September 30th, 1910." The plaintiff alleged that this undertaking was intended to operate as a revival of the old debt. Since then there had been further transactions between the parties, further sums having been lent on promis3ry notes and certain payments having been made by the defendant, but it was alleged that the amount claimed was still outstanding. Mr. Mainwaring gave evidence and strongly repudi- ated tbe idea that he accepted the composition, along with the other creditors. His acknowledgment of the £l4 received under that arrangement stated that it had been "placed to the credit of the defendant's account." Defendant's father was a large manufacturer and on his do ti left £200,000. Defendant's submission was that the old debt was included in the composition with his creditors. As to the undertaking to discharge the whole of his indebtedness he would not have signed it if be had thought it was to apply in the way the plaintiff alleged, lie was in a state of intoxication when he signed the undertaking. His Honour : Your allegation implies either that Mr. Mainwaring was guilty of something very tricky in tr 3 iog to get your tignature to something which might mean what you did not intend or else he got you to sign something which was wholly unnecessary. Defendant : Had I thoroughly understood it, I am certain I should not have signed it. Mr. Mainwaring was recalled by his Honour and said that, although the defendant might have had some drink when he signed the undertaking, be was competent to understand what he was signing. The document was read over to him. Mr 51ainwarieg indignantly repudiated the suggestion of trickery and said his conduct was sufficiently known in Warrington to give the lie to such an accusation. His Honour : The suggestion is that you were using the document to get out of the statute of limitations when the defendant never intended it to be wed for that purpose.

Plaintiff : I gave him a rough idea of what he owed at that pericd. I said " I will not allow you any furtle r moneys until you give me a note saying that what is due shall be paid on the day you receive your half-yearly income." Mr Lies said the case was full of peculiarities and iiiconsistencies, but he submitted that the whole con- uct of the case corroborated the defendants' story that ti.ere never wee any intention to revive the statute- barred debt. It was an extraordinary thing that Mr Mainwaring, if confident in his own mind that he intended to revive the debt by the acknowledgment which had been quoted, did not insert specific words to that effect in the document. Defendant submitted that when the composition was made Mr Mainwaring, in common with the other creditors, treated the matter as being at an end. His Honour said h had come to the conclusion that Mr Mainwaring did not agree to the composition and that the debt was not extinguished. The agreement of 1910 was intended by the plaintiff to operate ss a revival of the debt and be (His Honour) rejected the suggestion that Mr Mainwaring attempted to resort to a mean, dishonest and disgiaceful piece of trickery such as had been alleged. He believed Mr Mainwaring made it clear to the defendant that he was desirous of reviving the old debt which had never been extinguished but which bad become statute-barred. He also thought the defendant knew what he was about and that he signed the document intending it to be an acknowledgment to take the debt out of the statute. He gave judgment for the plaintiff for £44 16s. di. In view of the fact that an alteration in the claim was made after the action had been brought before the Court and that the defendant bad not the opportunity of knowing the exact particulars, his Honour did not award the plaintiff costs.

Politics and Personalities. The Attack on Mr. Crosfield.

Sir,—That worthy blue paper which represents the Women's Tariff Reform League cannot be compli- mented on its latest effusion against Mr. Crosfield. In a cynical and selfish world, it speaks well for him that be can be accused of no greater wrong-doing than that of dressing as a schoolboy at a baby party given by his wife. Hit is a crime to dress up, who offends more deeply than M. Harold Smith himself, who is constantly dressing up for the amusement of his party? It would perhaps be better if the Conservative member were to dress up his speeches instead of his person, to judge by his last performance in the House of Commons, on which occasion he received the snub he so richly deserved. It is no doubt highly flattering to Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield that their doings abroad should be so closely followed by the Tory party. All the more remarkable, then, that these acute observers should fail to notice that Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield also bad the pleasure of entertaining Sir Rufus Isaacs and Mr. Lloyd George in Cannes. Is it not strange that two such eminent statesmen should have honoured with their company a "would be" MP. given up to babyish amusements? But the Tory Party is evidently suffering under the defeat in the Town Hall Ward. It makes Mr. Harold Smith's tall talk about capturing every seat in the Council, sound so very silly, even for him. Let his supporters, however, devise some less childish method of contre..versy. It is an insult, not only to the War- rington electors, but to so great a sphere of work as politics, to think that minds can be distracted from the great issues of Free Trade, Home Rule, and so forth by such peurile attacks.—Yours etc., FAIR-MINDED.

div.head: "Money Lenders."
div.p: "Money Lenders."

Sir,—Some very significant statements were made in our local Police Court by the defending solicitor in the recent case of embezzlement.—" The prisoner got into the hands of money lenders. When men were in the hands of money lenders difficulties arose, and they did things which they should not do."—Here is one cf probably countless cases of honest men being gulled by the misleading and pernicious hand bills which these people carefully place in the houses of the w orkingclass. Walking Day will aeon be here, and the town will be flooded with another batch of these bills. " Strict privacy," "Note of hand," " no securities," &c.—All statements such as tempt a simple, but honest soul, to take the step to ruin. One sees poor women going to pay the usual remittance, with little prospect of ever lessening 'he load of debt which will ultiimately bring them into a similar position to that sad affair of last week. We have a Guild of Help in the town whose aims and objects are the advising and educating of the unfortunate. Would it not be a charity to circulate handbills warning people against the evils of which the solicitor spoke? if it is a fact, that this system makes men " do things which they should not do," ought not the Guild of Help to fight the system, and prercnt destitution, instead of patching it up after these unfortunates have fallen ? These thoughts may do some little good, and I will thank you if you can find space in your columns for their publication.— Yours r.C:3 ,

div.head: S. C. J.
div.p: S. C. J.

After-thoughts on Health Week. Sir,—lt is a good thing to notice in your columns that a great number of people have concentrated their attention upon the question of health for one week. It is a sign that people are becoming more conscious of the evils that surround us, and that more of us are asking : sihy these evils and which is the best way to obliterate them from our midst ? For after all the true wealth of a nation is not the quantity of money, or of millionaires, or building, or flests,or any material whatever it possesses, but, as John Ruskin tells us, the quantity of full-blooded, happy hearted human creatures. If this is wealth, then Great Britain is on the verge of bankruptcy. If we take a look at the figures upon status of our physique, those of us who do not habitually study these questions would, I feel sure, get a shock. The Inspector General of Recruiting tells us that in 1008 out 61,182 aspiring recruits examined, 17,960 were rejected. Not worth one shilling a day to shoot at —a percentage of 29 35. Again we are told by the Registrar General that in 1907 out of every thousand babies under one year 118 died. We also know that in some parts of rur industrial centres as many as one out of three babies born die,before they attain their first year of life. We also, know that about 60,000 people every year die of consumption, and it only needs ordinary observation for us to see that the people do not attain their proper physical develop- ment or live to their natural mature age. I believe the average span of life for the working class comes some- where near forty years. For the middle and upper classes it averages from about 5 5 to 60 years of life, in fact eve have come to such a pass "that healthy cid age" is a variety and net a natural end to life. Seeing an effect the sensible minded, must ask a cause. Some of us say hat the people do not practice hygienic living. They spit. They do not sleep with their windows open. They drink beer. They do not allow a current of air to go over their milk and the unscientific people like the Guild of Help just make a few superficial observa- tions and come to very superficial conclusions. I believe myself that if the people paid strict attention to every one of the items of advice given to them by our worthy friends the Guild of Help, it would only touch the fringe of the subject. I not not iv ish to decoy the efforts of anyone upon these terrible questions but eentiment (must be backed up by science nr ge to the wall. Now what are the causes of physical deterioration ? Speaking a few years ago Mr. John Burns, after quoting figures on housing congestion, said "The more people are multiplied in a given area, the more do they increase phthisis, tuberculosis, personal uncleanliness and immorality. So much for the effect of housing con- diticne. Again, the late Sir Henry Campbell Banner- man said "that the great concentration of human beings in dense masses is a state of things contrary to human nature, and that, unless powerful counter- attractive agencies were introduced, the issue was bound to be the suffering and gradual destruction of the mass of the population." At present, said Mr. Burns, one in seven of the population live at the rate of two in a room. In Manchester it is one in six. In Edinburgh one in three and Glasgow one in two. I believe there is no one who doubts that the bad housing is the great contributing cause of physical deterioration. Ancther great cause is the smoke dust, and chemicals emitted from our manufactories. Still another is adulteration of our food. And still another is the unhealthy conditions under which the working class work, and the bard grinding toil for wages not sufficient to maintain families in physical efficiency. After careful investigation Mr. Seebohm Ilowntree came to the conclusion that 30 per cent of our population did not receive a wage sufficient to maintain them in the barest necessities, and the wage he considered was necessary to procure the barest necessities is 21s. Bd. Never mind, we have an empire and navy. Can it be wondered that we need health weeks? But if this question is going to be tackled we want more than information about epitting and keeping our windows open. We want healthy homes, net brick boxes with slate lids as John Ruskin says. We want a pure food supply and purer air to breathe. I respectfully suggest that our Town Council should pure,hase all the cheap laud available upon the outskirts of the town, and there build homes worthy of our respect. Something must be done with our food supply. By way of inaugurating a common food supply,' suggest that steps betaken for the Council to take over the milk supply in the same manner as the water supply, and supply the people of Warrington with pure cheap milk. The private supply cf these things has failed. If the Council have not power to do these things the people of Warrington must send men to Parliament who will. Another important item is that the Council must use all their powers to suppress the great volume of smoke that continuously bangs over us like a black cloud. These are the lines along which we will have to go to cheek physical deterioration. At any rate that is the opinion of LABOR OMNIA.

Sir,—l am sure you will excuse me if I say that it was with feelings of pride and pleasure that the following letter was received. May its tone and p i urport nspire many Warringtonians to support the work of the committee in striving to study the welfare of those who otherwise might not have a fair chance in the battle of life.—Yours &e., W. H. J. JENKINS, Hon. Sec. [Copy.] Ammon()' New Zealand, April sth. The Sheffield police are trying to trace a gang of thieves who, by using public telephones, ordered Irides- men to send gocds to houses and then, posing. as shopkeepers' assistants, collected the goods, explaining that a mistake had been made.

The N.S.L. and Health. Sir, Ycur correspondent Mr. Dukes writing on "The National Servioa League and Health" deals with quite a number of questions, all of which,.one must assume, are more or less related, but are mixed so confusedly as to leave us in doubt with regaid to the real position of the writer. I lAt the on-set Mr. Dukes does make a specific s'ate- ment when he informs us that the Bpeaker4 at the N.S.L. meeting, held during health week "huedl to see that economic causes could be effectively combated by physical improvements only." No attempt is made to prove this statement. Why should an assumption be made that a speaker sees or fails to see" some- thing that he has not undertaken to speak about? As a matter of fact, each of the speakers would be quite prepared to admit that these "economic causes" to which Mr Dukes refers, are of great importance, but to expect them to be dealt with at a meeting arranged f-r discussion of the physical advantages of the N.S.L. prop: sills seems rather unreasonable. Mr. Dukes deals evasively with the matter and does not even attempt to tackle the question of the utility of universal ti aining for home defence, considered from the standpoint a improved physique cf the nation.

This question of physical fitness lies at the very basis of that of National defence. Its vital import- , tance will be seen if we depict in our thoughts what ' would happen under certain conditions. Let us imagine an extreme and shall we Fay improbable set of conditions, for example that through the ravages of consumption, of cancer, of intemperance and other destructive forces, the standard of health is so reduced that the sum total cf physical fitneis becomes only equal to one half the plesent standard. Under such conditions, we might have any number of Dread- noughts, and the general equipments of our Army and Navy might be of the best, but we should very s--,on be required thrQugh the operation of an immutable law, to give place to nations more fit to predominate and to survive. Ships and guns are useless without men, and men do not count for much unless they attain to a reasonable.standard of physical fitness. Everyone is bound to admit that the national physique could be considerably toned up by due atten- tion to the laws of health. It is important, that the rising generation especially, should have good food and should properly masticate it; that they should know the value of fresh air, and how to use their lungs so as to get a full supply, that proper exercise should be taken, and cleanlinei.s insisted on. The value of these things cannot be over-estimatel. And here we agree with Mr. Dukes when he affirms that there is a certain amount of knowledge of these subjects evcn among the poorest of the people. But a fact that we think deserves emphasis is this, that there are 'thousands of our young people (thanks to improved methods of education), that have some knowledge of these things and yet they do not use the knowledge they 'have, to the best advantage. We believe that these persons and also many who unfortunately are t f a more ignorant type would receive incalculable benefit from such a scheme as the N.S.L. proposes. Proper discipline and the toning up that would result from the knowledge that these things are not only good and useful, but must be attended to, would be worth more to cur young men than anything else we know of. Even Mr. Duke must admit that three or four months open air life near the sea, or the mountains, under discipline which would necessitate proper expansion of the lungs, with plenty of general exercise would not only brace up and strengthen our young men, but would teach them experimentally the value of these things, so that in many cases they would as far as p)ssible take advantage of later opportunities, and results would be achieved which would not be likely to follow any ordinary or haphazard methods. Yours truly,
G. DALE.

An interesting ceremony took place on Sunday last, when the "Meritorious Service Medal " (of which only a limited number are allotted to eac4 regiment) was presented on the church parade, in Orford Barracks, to ex-Quartermaster-Sergeant J.Faulks, now residing at 201, Padgate-laue, Warrington, who has s•>rved for over 30 years in the 80th Foot (now the South Staffordshire Regiment) and in the Army Pay Corps (Military Staff Clerks Section). Quartermaster-Sergeant Faulks took part in the Perak campaign, N.W. Frontier (India) 1875-6, Zulu War 1878-9, and holds, together with the Medal for Long Service and Good Conduct, the Medals and Clasps given for these campaigns. With the addition of the Meritorious Medal he is now in possession of four medals. He euli-ted on the 24th August, 1870, and was discharged en pension on the 31st July, 1001. The Meritorious Service Medal is practically the highest hoinur that can be granted to N.C.O '8 and men of Ffis Majesty's service.

div.head: DEATH OF DR. CHARLES WHITE J.P.
div.p: DEATH OF DR. CHARLES WHITE J.P.
AN ACTIVE AND USEFUL LIFE.

Warrington is the poorer for the death of Dr, Charles White, J.P., who passed away somewhat suddenly at his residence, Holly House, Sankey-street, , at 10.45 on Saturday night. Although he had reached the ripe rid age of 82—he would have been 83 if he had lived until June 2nd the doctor retained an alertness and vigour of mind and body which many a younger man might envy, and to the last he took such a keen interest in the many-sided activities r.f the town with which be had been so long associated, that he will be greatly missed by all classes of the com- munity. A great believer in outdoor exercise, it was his cus.om to take a daily walk into the country. usually accompanied by one or more of his , daughters. On Friday. rimming he went to Stockton Heath and on returbing appeared to be over-tired. Disquieting symptoms developed in the afternoon and Dr. Langdale was called in. He was unremitting in his attentions, but the aged drctor was beyond human aid and the end came peacefully in the presence of the members of the family and one or two very in imate friends. It was with a sense of profound regret that the general public heard of the prssing from their midst of this venerable and respected figure, while to many the news came as a heavy personal loss. Although singularly outspoken and n,t without. a touch of the autocratic, the doctor was one of the most lovable of friends. His wide knowledge and his terse and happy way of expressing his thoughts mode it a delight and privilege ti hold intimate coaverse witb him, and na-one was re idier to discern and reward true merit wherever he found it. The words" a fine ell English gentleman " were never more fittingly applied than in his case. He had always a smile and cheery greeting and, while he held strong views on some subjects, he was c mrteous and kindly tAvards those wh did n see eye-to-eye with him.

Dr. White, who was born at Doncaster in the year 1829, received his medical training at Guy's Hospital. Having taken the degree of M.R.C.B.' he came to War- rington in 1853, succeeding the late Dr. Bickerton as house surgeon at the old Dispensary in Buttermarket- street. Ia 1862 he took up a private practice in Academy-street, but all his life he continued warmly devoted to the interests of the Infirmary and never lost an opportunity of advocating its claims upon public generosity. When he ceased to be house surgeon he was appointed hon. surgeon and later con- sulting surgeon. These offices he subsequently relinquished, but continued to give valuable service as a vice-president of the institution and a member of the House Visitors' and Fioanca Committee. He made it one of the guiding principles of his life never to undertake offices which he was not prepared to fulfil to the letter, and his regularity and punctuality at meetings set a notable example. He was particularly appreciative of the efforts of the Infirmary Working- men's Committee, bit retiring from medical practice at the age of 70, Dr. White was the recipient of a beautiful rose bowl and silver salver from his colleagues in the profession. Needless to say, he treasured the gifts most highly. Dr White was a conspicuously loyal and devoted member of the Church of England and was deeply attached to the Parish Church, where he had worshipped throughout his long connection with War- rington. Every Sunday morning found him in his place at church, and no climatic severities deterred him from discharging that religious duty. Even when snow was thick on the ground and many younger people would not venture away from the fireside, the doctor was to be seen trudging along the street to the old chu.ch which he loved so well. He served as aidesman during part of the time that the Hon. and Rev. Horace Powys was rector, and subsequently for a brief period during the reczorship of the Rev. William Quekett. Be was also a member of the old Church Institute. From 1803 to 1901 Dr. White was medical officer of the Training C,llege and his retire- ment was a cause of regret to all connected with that important institution. The esteem in which he ' was held found expression in the presentation to him of a Gladstone hag and four silver candlesticks. The doctor, in return for tie kindness extended to him, presented the college with a photograph rf himself. This was subsequently reproduced in the college magazine—the only occasion, we believe, on which the doctor, who always shunned anything which appeared to him to savour of ostentation or advertise- ment, allowed his portrait to be published. In his earlier days Dr White was a surgeoa major in the Smith Lancashire Militia, under the command of the late Col. Ireland-Blackburne, and he attended the manccuvres which were held at Cannock Chase in 1873. He was away from Warrington for about a month and threw himself with thoroughness and enthusiasm into the work of the camp. The doctor was a keen supporter of the Warrington Savings Bank and was never tired of commending it to the workingclasses as an (incentive to thrift. He was a trustee of the Blue Coat school and was a welcome visitor whenever he attended to distribute the prizes or transact other bu-iness of the institution, A great lover of music, he made a point of attending classical concerts and no one did more to encourage the work of the Musical Society. with which his late wife was at one time identified. He rarely missed a concert and did everything in his power to advance the interests of the society which he regarded as a high educational influence. Dr. White was a man of literary culture and also possessed an extensive knowledge of scientific subjects. He was a much-valued member of the Literary and Philosophical Society, as well as of the Field Club, and had acted as president of each for several years. His intervention in the discussions was welcomed, for he was always able to strike an interesting and original note, and he never hesitated to express himself with a frankness which sometimes took the form of caustic criticism. Apart from his strtetly professional work, his scientific knowledge lay chin fly in the realm of geology,but he was also a keen student of natural history and even when past his eightieth year was able to wax as enthusiastic as ever about the discovery of some rare specimen of bird or plant life in the neighbourhood. Dr. White was appointed a justice of the peace for the borough by the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster in 1885 and for Lancashire (West Darby Hundred), on July 11th, 1905. He devoted himself to his magisterial duties with characteristic diligence and conscientiousness, seeking to make use of his position to speak that" word in season" which might arrest the downward course of a prisoner capable of ref ,rmation.
He married in 1863 Annie (daughter of the late Dr. Greenup, of Farnworth), who died on May 12,h, 1875. He leaves three daughters, his only son having died in 1809.
THE FUNERAL.

Touching simplicity characterised the funeral of the late Dr. White which took place at the Warring- ton Cemetery at noon on Thursday. The large gathering, representative of all seztins of the towns- people, was in itself an eloquent tribute to the affec- tionate regard in which the deceased gentleman was held, and of the widespread de,ire to pay tribute to his memory. The cortege proceeded direct from Efolly House to the Cemetery. At the gates the choir of the Parish Church, under the direction of Mr. F. M. Darby, Mud. Ban., was in waiting, and as the mcurners passed along the drive to the

chapel, the Easter hymn "Jesus Lives" was sung. First came a posse of the Borough police, in charge of Inspector Hodgkiss, then the clergy and choir of the Parish Church and echolars of the Blue Coat school, with the superintendent, Mr. E. Rose. Following the mourners, walked the Mayor and members of the Corporation and representatives of various organisa- tions. The clergy taking part in the service were the Rector (Rev Canon Willis), Revs. Canon Stevenson, E gr 4. Carleton, J. A. Bratt and T. Vickers. AN APPRECIATION.

An attr?ctive specimen of a manly man was Charles White (who never liked the courtesy title of Doctor), the like of whom one seldom meets in many a long day's march. The startling news of his sudden passing, came upon us with all the shock of a cutting chill. It is difficult to realise that we have indeed for the last time seen his familiar face and form, and,with faltering faith, try to understand that 'all is for the best." The " mystery " as he termed it, had no terrors for him. He freely discussed the inevitable with rare corn- nosure and resignation, and to the very end be quitted himself like a man. A sterling type of virility was Charles White. An honourable colleague, a good parent, a sound citizen, an admirable and loyal friend ; conscientious always, well read and well informed, logical and thorough ; a close reasoner, endowed with much natural ability and shrewd commonsense, having the courage of his opinions, which he could express with lucidity and force; always himself, never unduly influenced by weight of opposition or its source; his remarks candidly reflected his own nature, views and thoughts. He was a m,an of strong religious and political con- victions, consistently and rigidly living up to them. There was never any discoid between his profession and his practice. Straightforward in all his dealings, he had no toleration for the invertebrate time-server, or subter- fuge in any form; he hated humbug, but was by no means devoid of charity for the foibles and follies that mark us as " desperately human. " Mentally clear- sighted, transparently sincere,of unswerving rectitude, genial, companionable and capable, judged by the standards which men use in judging each other, the record comes out "all right.' Such was Charles White--" nothing extenuate, nor set down aught in malice." J. It. Y. MAGISTERIAL REFERENCE.

Before the ordinary business began at the Borough Police Court, on Monday, fitting tribute was paid to the memory of Dr. White. The Mayor, who presided, said the town generally, and the Bench in particular, had sustained a great loss by the removal of Mr. White, who for 59 years had been associated with the medical, social and intellectual life of the district. He had known Mr. White for 33 years, and would never forget the kind- ness which he received from him in the early years of his residence in Warrington. Their late colleague was a man of outstanding characteristics and admirable qualities. He always had the courage of his convictions, and whether in his capacity as a magistrate or as a private gentleman thoroughness stamped his words and deeds throughout. He deplored the loss of a sincere friend, for whom he had an unswervingly high respect, and he tendered his humble and sincere condolences to the bereaved relatives. Mr. Arthur Browne, on behalf of the sol:citors practising at the Court, associated himself with the expression of sympathy and regret. He spoke of his long acquaintance with Mr. White, and remarked that, though he was wont to be somewhat brusque, he was at the same time most kindhearted. They deeply mourned his loss, and would greatly miss his cheery countenance.

THE RECTOR'S TRIBUTE. Preaching at the Parish Church on Sunday evening, the Rector said he was sate the congregation would not wish him to conclude his sermon without a few words in reference to one of the oldest and most respected inhabitants of their town,the late Dr. Charles White. He would refer to a few features of his character, which specially struck him. First as to his intellectuality. He was a great reader, possessed a wide knowledge of things in general, and had an intelligent grasp of many subjects. Morally he was straighforward, upright, and most conscientious. He was also what might be termed a " down- right " man, very outspoken and courageous, a good man of business, and always punctual to the moment. Daring an acquaintance of twenty-four years, he had never known him a minute late at any engagement. He would have thought it very wrong to waste any man's time, and he felt his own to be precious, too. Socially, he was the most genial and pleasant of companions, and the kindest and truest of friends. Be was a deeply religious God•fearing man, a devoted and most generous Churchman, and always ready to help a worthy cause and a deserving case. A few years ago he received warning that his powers were failing, a warning not unheeded, but he continued steadfast in ' the performance of all duties within his power, was rigid in his observance of Sunday, and was never absent in the moping from church. On Friday last he overtired himself in his favourite exercise of walking, but on Saturday he recovered. At ten

div.p: ST. GEORGE'S MISSION.

Before giving the address at St. George's Mission on Sunday evening, Mr. 11. J. Westbrook (who was taking duty there) said Dr. White was a conscientious and consistent Churchman, and his example was a constant sermon to those who belonged to the younger generation, but who by gaps such as the present were rapidly stepping to vards tho front ranks. A medical man had it in hia power to do an incalculable amount of good, both religiously and sccially, and the late Dr. White was amongst those who might fairly be styled followers of Luke, the beloved physician and friend of St. Paul. He had been called by God to a higher sphere of labour, and had left them an example that they might follow in his steps.

I promised last week to give directions for mount- ing maps in sections, thus saving 50 to 60 per cent. in their cost. Although said to be "mounted on linen," calico is always used, price 2d. a yard. Duster cloth, butter muslin or art muslin is the best, as it contains no dressing, and that is a very important item if ycu want the paste t) stick permanently. Stretch it slightly with pins on a dresser top for the mounting. The size of the sections all depends on the size of your pocket. The depth of your pocket,for once, doesn't matter. If you do a bit of poaching, you can have them a gocd deal larger than if you happen to be a lady. Mine are abcut 7x 5 inches, or Bartholomew's sheets cut into IS. Of course you must divide the sheets equally in both directions, and carefully get them in their right order. Don't wet them beforehand. Now for the paste. Two table- spoonfulls heaped with 11 ur, and mixed with cold water to the consistency of furniture cream, the thicker the better. It is then boiled and stirred the Vi hole time with a good strong wrist and a good strong spoon. At the end it is almost solid. It must be blushed on to a board or slate or sheet of glass, and when a good thick even layer has been obtained, each section in turn is laid on it and smoothed out. About an eighth of an inch between the sections will be best for your first map, or the sections will not come straight, and thee the edges will fray up with folding. The beautiful colouring of Bartholomew's maps makes them into works of art, and if you get the edition that the C.T.C. officials have revised, you have the quality of the roads given as well as their direction and height, all the dangerous gates marked, and hundreds of things or places of interest that the Ordnance maps omit. Dolgelly is the southern centre of North Wales, just as Llandudno is the not thorn. But what a con- trast ! One all artificiality, the other a town of nature. Llandndno is an English town where hardly a word of Welsh is spoken in the s`lops ; Dolgelly is Welsh to the core and all the business is transacted in the native tongue, and althcugh evetyone in town can talk to you in either language, a good walk into the country will put you in many a place where you will find adults who cannot speak a word of English. One could fill this column with the most meagre descrip- tion of what the cyclist ought to see around this unique town right at the foot of Cader Idris, but I will return to the subject next week. I have often been asked for the best route from Warrington to Southport. The great trouble is cross- ing St. Helens, and one cannot be surptised at tourists wanting to avoid it. Sheet Bof Bartholomew's half inch map shows the following road very plainly, which avoids Prescot as well. Instead of turning right at Bold, keep straight on through Rainhill village. The fourth turn to the right past the station, or the seci.nd after the Church takes you up past some large red sandstone quarries. Then go down the second road on the left, over the railway, across the Prescot-St. Helens main road to the supply reservoirs for Liver- pool, and along the east side of Knowsley Park. In about 21 miles the road bends west, but instead of I Mowing the finger post to Rainford, go straight on till you reach the north gate of the park. There present the permit you will have received in advance from the steward by writing, and four miles of the mr-st beautiful road awaits you. Splendid banks of rhododendrons line one side, and miles of fields on the other,reminding you again of Cheshire. Another four miles of high read and 3,, u are in Ormskirk, with Southport eight miles ahead. What a difference in the lot of the cyclist since the eighties ! 'The first time I cycled to Southport, every inch of road for miles round was paved with cobbles, with a narrow track for walkers at the side. We rode in the track, but at the risk Of catching the pedal (fixed as they all were) in the tall grass clumps at every stroke. It was the :same on the road to Blackpool and Lytham, Fleet- wood and Morecambe. And then folk say, "Oh, cycling is not what it used to be since these horrid motors have come on the roads !" Why, no greater blessing ever was bestowed on the cyclist than the motor car and the auto-cycle ! I will return to that subject some other day. I was struck with a new carrier that was shown me last week, the " Wiaeberg." It fete practically any cycle, needs no stays, and folds up against your ' back forks under your tool bag, making a very neat cape carrier. They are said to be good for 501b5., and I believe it, though they certainly are not heavy. The price is 2s. 3d. and 2s. 9d. The " Wineberg tyre-raiser, Od. is well worth seeing by those who ride wired-on covers. If you try it, you will see it has needed some thinking out. Lamp time (Lancashire and Cheshire), to-night 19.5 next Saturday 0.16. WARRINGTON WEiLEYAN CYCLE CLUB,

The tide on Saturday May 11th should have been to Hale Cliff on the Mersey north shore. But we are out for pleasure more than work, so we asked to be excused facing that westerly gale. We turned right round, and used the wind to such good effect that we reached Glazebury by four o'clock. Tea for 15 was served at Mrs. Mark's, the C.T.C. caterer, and she will oertainly be asked to do us the same good turn again when we next go to Chatmoss. Aber tea we had a charming walk over the peat moss, and a good many 1,-,stria ferns were brought home from the ditch sides. The return was made by Warburton Bridge, Heatley and Broomedge, and as usual after tea, the wind had dropped to a great extent, and we felt tho same satisfaction that one feels after dodging an unwel- come acquaintance who cannot otherwise be got rid of. Thus we proved the value of our new rule, which we rec..mmend to other clubs : " The Captain in charge shall hsve power to change the runs (considering wind &c.), according to the discretion of the majority present at the start, but shall leave intimation at the advertised starting point." SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEY GUILD CYCLE

CLUB. In charming weather on Saturday last we turned our wheels in the direction of Arley, twenty of our members turning out, the road taken being the one that leads on to Knutsford, and the return journey through Crowley and Appleton. After reaching Arley a house was soon found where they were quite willing to cater for our wants very reasonab'y. Several of the members, who have a desire for fresh air treatment, had the pleasure of dining under the canopy of the heavens. After tea a ramble rouud the lake was a pleasing feature The country side is now so very beautiful that it is with regret we think of the pleasure we miss by having neglected to spare a little of our time in the study of botany. Nevertheless, nature had to give up some of her treasures, for although we only spent about an hour there, a considerable quantity of wild flowers of different varieties were gathered and taken home. A pleasant j3urney home brought an enjoy- able outing to a close.

THE CANADIAN ACTING TRADE AGENT at Berlin recently stated in a report to the Department of Trade and Commerce at Ottawa that the stream of Gernan emigration is likely to turn Canada-wards. The agent points out that his office, under the German law, is not permitted to induce a German subject to emigrate, but information may be given, and has been given, in response to numerous enquiries from people" who have decided to go to Canada, nearly all of whom are in com- fortable circumstances and many with a considerable amount of money to invest."
